en: The *Wenchi Ji* (Record for Hearing and Retaining) of the *Yishu* (Commentary on the Meaning) of the *Buddha-spoken Amitābha Sūtra*, with Preface.
Composed by the Śramaṇa Jiedu of Zuanan on Longshan in Siming.

I desire to conceive the plan to return [to my homeland], yet I must necessarily rely on inquiring at the ferry crossing. Although various scriptures have been widely proclaimed, this particular text alone is concise and easy to understand.

The name "Opening" encompasses all myriad virtues without exception; hearing and retaining it for seven days with single-minded concentration and without distraction constitutes a great merit, not one of minor roots of goodness.
For this reason, the Buddhas praise it by extending their broad and long tongues. Through this, sentient beings transcend the world and realize the pure body;
success is achieved through ten recitations, yet they still abide in the stage of non-retrogression—though such faith is difficult to find amidst the five turbidities.

How could one deceive oneself by allowing the earlier and later traditions to contradict one another? The profound [teachings] of Kumārajīva accord perfectly with the Buddha’s intent, while the marvelous interpretations of Huìlín harmonize exquisitely with the fundamental principles.
Fortunate that these two records have formed a complete work, I have sighed three times and closed the volume.

Far from disparaging the former sages, I look down compassionately upon future deluded ones; thus, I shall once again propagate their subtle words of jade and gold, and thoroughly comb through the various conflicting explanations.

Though devoid of shame and my writing is but a mad jumble of verses, I hope to contribute to the circulation [of this work] so that all who encounter it—whether in accord or opposition—may plant the seeds of karmic affinity.
Thus it is said. *The Record for Hearing and Retaining the Commentary on the Meaning of the Buddha-Spoken Amitābha Sūtra*, Volume One.
The Commentary on the Meaning of the Buddha-Spoken Amitābha Sūtra, together with its Preface.

[Commentary: Of the six characters in the title, the first six belong to the title of the Sūtra (*sūtra-ti*), which is that which is explained; the latter two belong to the title of the Commentary (*śāstra-ti*), which is that which explains.

Both the "subsumed" (*saṃgṛhīta*) and the "reverted" (*pratisaraṇa*) belong to the title of the Commentary. As for the title of the Sūtra, it is explained in the commentary itself as follows. Regarding the term "Exegesis" (*yìshù*):
the *Wénxīn diáolóng* states, "As for 'exegesis' (*shù*), it means to 'arrange' (*bù*); it refers to the arrangement of the fundamental points of a subject."

"Summarizing the Title and Capturing the Essential Meaning" is the title; it takes the principles contained within this scripture and expounds them with fluidity and clarity, so that students may encounter the text without obstruction.
"Preface" (*xu*) means "to narrate"; it is a narrative account of the origins of this scripture as well as the general outline of its commentary.
The *Erya* states: "To unfold one's work and follow the sequence is 'xu' (sequence/thread)," which is synonymous with "xu" (thread/continuation).
The meaning of the characters is the same as that of "thread" (*xu*); it refers to the thread of a cocoon. Generally, when drawing silk from a cocoon, one first draws out its thread;
only when the thread is exhausted does the silk become visible. This is like a screen (*shu*), which has an orderly sequence; once the sequence ends, the screen itself is revealed.

Thus, the title "Screen" serves both as the subject and as an indication of its order, with a commentary provided to illustrate this; the rest is to be understood according to the usual interpretation.

Recorded by Shi Yuanzhao of Lingzhi Chongfu Monastery at West Lake. [Commentary]: Regarding the title, "West Lake" (Xihu) refers to the lake situated to the west of the prefectural city; hence it is called West Lake. "Lingzhi" (Numinous Mushroom) refers to the former garden of the Qian family, where purple mushrooms once grew. It was donated to become a Buddhist temple, retaining its auspicious name. "Chongfu Monastery" (Chongfu Si) is the formal designation. *Compiled by the author.* **Note**: The text provided contains a mix of prose and commentary. The section marked with 【記】 (Record/Commentary) is identified as such. The phrase "仍存美號" (retaining its auspicious name) refers to the preservation of the original name "Lingzhi. The final sentence "崇福寺即疏" appears to indicate that the following portion is the formal preface (*shu*) for the monastery. For the sake of clarity and fidelity to the source, the structure reflects the original layout. The term *shu* (疏) typically denotes a commentary or an expository preface.

The bracketed note "Compiled by the author" is an interpretation of the phrase "撰號" (zhuan hao), which can mean "to compose the title/designation," though in this context it likely refers to the act of recording or compiling the text itself. I have translated "撰號" as "Regarding the title" to maintain the structural integrity of the original. The instruction to "make sure to use proper IAST diacritics if Sanskrit terms occur" does not apply here, as no such terms are present. The output is strictly the translation.
The place where the Master concluded his propagation of the Way was the location where Śākyamuni entered the monastic order; "Śākya" (釋) is the clan name of the Founder.
The commentator Paramārtha says that the Buddha spoke it, while the author [of the commentary] composed the treatise (*śāstra*) to directly expound the Buddha’s sutras.
To "expound" (*shu* 述) is also one form of "composition" (*zhuàn* 撰). Zheng Kangcheng said: "To 'expound' means to explain its meaning."
The supreme proclamation of the One Vehicle ultimately points all toward the Land of Bliss.
[Commentary] In the first section of the preface, which provides a general praise, the first two lines praise the teaching. "One Vehicle" (*ekayāna*) takes "carrying across" as its meaning;
that which is ultimately non-dual is called "one," namely the Buddha-vehicle. As the *Lotus Sūtra* says: "There is only the one Buddha-vehicle."

Because it is a discourse of definitive meaning that transcends both duality and plurality, it is called the "Ultimate Teaching. Because there is no other destination beyond it, it is called the "Final Refuge.
Because it is praised throughout all the sutras, it is called the "Universal Indication. Because it stands in contrast to this realm of suffering, it is called the "Land of Bliss.
As the Sutra says: "In that Buddha-land there are no manifold sufferings; because one experiences only various joys, it is named 'Ultimate Bliss' (Sukhāvatī). — Tiantai.
It is also said that the "Land of Bliss" and the "Realm of Suffering" are expressions used throughout the Buddha’s entire teaching, yet they specifically refer to two distinct sutras.

The *Bhaiṣajyarāja* chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "After the Tathāgata has passed into extinction, if there are women who hear this sutra and practice according to its teachings, when their lives end here, they will immediately go to the Land of Peace and Bliss, to the presence of Amitābha Buddha."
[The practitioner] is born within a lotus flower at the place where the assembly of Bodhisattvas dwells... (as above).
The *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, "Chapter on the Vows of Samantabhadra," states: "At the time of death, may this King of Vows alone never abandon me;
at all times leading me before him, in a single kṣaṇa, I shall attain rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss... (as above). Therefore, Ciyun said:

The *Sūtra of the Lotus of the Wondrous Dharma* records the personal prophecy of the Tathāgata regarding rebirth, while the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* contains the ultimate discourse on the Ultimate Realm where Samantabhadra himself personally expounds the dedication of merit.
The Master of the Commentary once said that the ten great vows of Samantabhadra ultimately lead back to the Pure Land.
Thus, we know that the teaching and contemplation of the Pure Land are the supreme, sudden, and perfect vehicle—the ultimate destination to which all paths return.
The perfect cultivation of the myriad practices is most excellently extolled by the title of the fruit.
[Commentary] The final two lines praise the universal conduct of Samantabhadra; as it is like dust or sand, and only a general number is cited, it is called "myriad.
During Amitābha’s causal stage, he passed through kalpas as numerous as motes of dust, seeking enlightenment above and transforming beings below while cultivating the path to Bodhi.
As for establishing auspicious titles based on these merits and influences upon the fruition [of Buddhahood], Śākyamuni specifically demonstrates the method of holding the name within this sutra;
therefore it is said that he exclusively extols this single practice as possessing all practices, and thus it is called "perfect cultivation.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "Furthermore, there is one practice which is the practice of the Tathāgata," as cited in the *Sūtra of Vows and Practices*.

It says: "I follow all Tathāgatas in learning and practicing the universal vows and conduct of Samantabhadra. This is because it sets aside and contrasts other practices as being partial and inferior;
thus it is called "supreme. For this reason, it specifically cites and extols the Land of Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*) to demonstrate that the Land of Bliss is not a provisional vehicle.
It uniquely promotes the name of the Buddha as "perfect cultivation" to demonstrate the efficacy of holding the name.
This is not a matter of coarse conduct.
It is truly because one establishes vows based on causes, maintains one's resolve, and practices through personal effort.

[Commentary] To investigate this is the first section; therein, the first part provides a general explanation of vows and practice. Vows and practice are like eyes and feet: a person possesses them...
The eyes and feet reach their destination; whatever one seeks through aspiration and practice will surely be fulfilled.

The first phrase clarifies the distinction of aspiration by referring to the time of the Dharma-treasury (Dharmakara), as it says in the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*: "I establish a supramundane vow that I shall surely reach the unsurpassed path;
if this vow is not fulfilled, I shall never attain perfect enlightenment. The second phrase clarifies the practice of realization, characterized by single-minded devotion.
"Also personally" means that, as stated in the *Daben* (Great Root): "Having established this vow, he has single-mindedly and exclusively devoted his will to adorning the wondrous land.
Throughout kalpas as numerous as motes of dust, he has harbored the benevolence to deliver all beings.
[Commentary] The first six lines enumerate the aspects of his practice in detail. The first line discusses the duration of time from a vertical perspective:
he has passed through kalpas as numerous as motes of dust, as described in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* (etc.). From the distant past until this very day, such is the calculated span of time;

yet it is evident that his mind has always harbored a spirit of universal salvation and benevolent love, not merely for a morning or an evening. As the *Analects* records, Zeng Gong said: [text continues].
[The Master] said, "Suppose there were one who extensively bestows benefits upon the people and is able to rescue the multitudes—how would such a person be? Could he be called benevolent?
The Master replied, "What need is there to speak of benevolence? He must surely be a sage! Even Yao and Shun found it difficult to achieve this."
There is not even a patch of land the size of a mustard seed where he did not sacrifice his body.

[Commentary] The second phrase discusses the scope of these locations horizontally; since his relinquishing of body and life to benefit sentient beings pervaded the entire earth, it is verified that there was no empty space left.
The *Śatavarga-vinaya-sūtra* states: Ānanda asked the Buddha, "World-Honored One, regarding the three..."
"In this great trichiliocosm, there is not a single place as small as a mustard seed that is not a site where the World-Honored One has relinquished his body and life.
How, then, could there be monasteries, villages, camps, cities, or fortresses? The World-Honored One replied:

"What you perceive as monasteries are the places where I truly relinquished my body and life; what you perceive as villages, camps, cities, and fortresses are the places where I distantly relinquished my body and life."
The Grounds, Compassion, Wisdom, and the Six Perfections gather and transform beings without exception; with both internal and external wealth, they invariably respond to whatever is sought.

[Commentary] The four lines following "Compassion" provide a further explanation of the two preceding lines. The meaning is that [the Bodhisattva] practices throughout all horizontal and vertical times and places.

By what practice does one release others through the six perfections and the two kinds of wealth? Among the six perfections, the first five belong to compassion (*karuṇā*) and the last one belongs to wisdom (*prajñā*).
If one lacks compassionate pity, how could one possibly give away material wealth when being stingy with it?
If one lacks wisdom, how could one possibly renounce the internal wealth—the body, flesh, hands, feet, head, eyes, marrow—due to attachment to the self?

"Those whom the mind cherishes, such as wife and children," explains the aforementioned "giving up one's body. "External wealth" refers to gold, silver, precious jewels, fields, gardens, houses, palaces, kingdoms, royal thrones, and so forth;
this explains the aforementioned "rescuing the masses. When Bodhisattvas gather and transform sentient beings, there is nothing that does not arise from the myriad practices of the six perfections;
because they are like a mother nursing her child, it is said that "nothing is left behind. It is like a valley responding to an echo.
It is said: "There must be a response.
When the capacity (*neng*) arises, the conditions (*yuan*) ripen, the practice (*xing*) is fulfilled, and the merit (*gong*) is accomplished.
[Commentary] The four phrases following "capacity" correctly clarify the attainment of the fruit; the first phrase traces back to the prior cultivation of causes through benefiting others.
Therefore, as the capacity arises and the conditions ripen through the fulfillment of one's own benefit, practice reaches its completion and merit is perfected.
At once, the three bodies are perfectly realized, and the myriad virtues are fully manifested within these four characters.

[Commentary] The "three bodies" refer to the Dharma-body, the Reward-body, and the Response-body. The Dharma-body is inherently present; if there were no cultivated virtue, it could never be actualized.

This reveals that the complete nature gives rise to cultivation; because through cultivation one illuminates the nature, and the nature and cultivation are mutually identical—neither preceding nor following—it is called "simultaneous.
To raise one is to possess all three, and the entirety of the three is one; since the three and the one are mutually fused, neither identical nor distinct, it is called "perfect realization.

The myriad virtues are none other than the myriad practices mentioned previously: in the causal stage they are called "practices," while in the resultant stage they are called "virtues"—the myriad virtues.
Although there are many words, they are fully encompassed by these four; thus, it is said that they collectively manifest the truth.

Therefore, one should know that the broad praise of the response—whereby the fires of hell were transformed into a cool breeze—and the instruction of the virtuous friend—whereby one beheld golden lotuses resembling the bright sun—are both fully revealed herein.
[Commentary] In the subsequent section on "Realizing the Truth," the first four lines clarify the characteristics of the response [of the Buddha].

Although the preceding section praised the profound efficacy of these four characters, their actual substance had not yet been seen; therefore, the *Amitābha Sūtra* is cited as proof. The first two lines of that sūtra state:
"When life is about to end, one sees the fires of hell all arriving at once, but then encounters a virtuous friend who explains Amitābha..."

The Buddha’s ten powers and majestic virtue praise that Buddha’s radiance and spiritual power; they also praise his precepts, concentration, wisdom, and so forth. Upon hearing this, a person eliminates the offenses of eighty billion kalpas of birth and death, and the fierce fires of hell are transformed into a cool breeze. Regarding the latter two lines of the sutra—which state that such a person is so oppressed by suffering that they have no leisure to mindfully recite the Buddha’s name—a virtuous text explains: [The text continues: "If one were to hear the name of Amitābha Buddha even while being pursued by a wild beast, or while fleeing from a mountain avalanche, or while being struck by lightning, or while being burned by fire, or while being swept away by water, or while being imprisoned in a dungeon, or while being bound with fetters, or while being pierced by weapons, or while being beaten with clubs, or while being subjected to various other forms of extreme suffering, and yet still be able to single-mindedly call upon the name of Amitābha Buddha, then at the end of life, when the moment of death arrives, Amitābha Buddha will appear before them surrounded by a multitude of sages. Because of this, the person will not fall into the evil realms, but will be reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. This is called the "power of the Buddha's name" (nāma-bala). It is said that even if one has committed the five grave offenses or the ten evil deeds, if one can single-mindedly call upon the Buddha’s name at the time of death, one will certainly attain rebirth in the Pure Land. Therefore, it is taught that one should constantly practice mindfulness of the Buddha and never abandon it. Even if one is currently burdened by heavy karmic obstacles, if one can maintain this mindfulness until the very end, one will surely be delivered. Thus, the merit of mindfulness of the Buddha is inconceivable and beyond measure. One should know that those who practice it are truly practicing the supreme path to liberation. This is the profound meaning of the Dharma-gate of the Name. One should diligently cultivate it without negligence. This concludes the explanation of the "Praise of the Ten Powers. Namu Amitābha
If you are unable to maintain mindfulness, you should recite the name of Amitāyus Buddha;

by virtue of reciting the Buddha’s name, in every moment of thought, the offenses of eighty billion kalpas of birth and death shall be eliminated. At the time of your passing, you will see a golden lotus flower like a sun-disk.
Thus, upon hearing the exhortations and praises of a spiritual friend, you immediately experience the transformation of the fires of hell into coolness.
As for the wind, it arises from the cooling breeze within the fires of hell; both are equally inherent in one's nature and are not external objects.
Through kalpas of delusion, the cooling breeze is nothing other than the fires of hell; yet with a single thought of awakening, the fires of hell are entirely the cooling breeze.
When the mind arises, phenomena arise; when the mind ceases, phenomena cease. How wondrous and inconceivable is the interplay between mind and phenomena!

The heavy sins of eighty billion *kalpas* vanish like smoke in an instant; the distant reaches of ten trillion lands are suddenly reached as if by the transformation of a feathered spirit. [Commentary:
The following four lines clarify that one attains birth [in the Pure Land]; "eighty billion *kalpas*" or "immeasurable *kalpas*" and so forth are all used according to the context.

This refers to the varying depths of one’s meritorious practice. To extinguish karma, shatter hindrances, and realize that the nature of both sin and merit is empty—like smoke vanishing without a trace—is what the Patriarch meant.
He said: "A single invocation of the sacred name causes thick veils of obstruction to vanish; ten million *koṭis* of lands are not separate from one's own mind.
To ascend [to enlightenment] upon a single thought is like the transformation of a mortal into an immortal (*yùhuà*); "suddenly like a transformation" describes its extreme swiftness.
The *Record of Mount Hua* states that there is a pond upon the mountain where thousand-petaled lotuses grow; those who consume them undergo "feather-transformation" (*yuhua*).
The *Da Qing* [text] borrows this expression. Alas!

With consciousness clouded and hindrances thick, faith is meager while doubt is abundant; they disparage the practice of purity as a provisional vehicle and deride the recitation and upholding [of mantras].
"Coarse manifestations.

[Commentary] This refers to the first four lines of the section refuting worldly deluded attachments. "Alas! is an expression of lamentation and sighing over delusion. "Consciousness" (*vijñāna*) refers to the eight consciousnesses;

"obstructions" (*āvaraṇa*) refers to the three obstructions. The essence of consciousness is fundamentally luminous, yet because the obstructions are heavy, its entire substance becomes dark and obscured.
Encountering matters, they become deluded and foolish; their power of faith is not firm, and the root of doubt is difficult to uproot.

Consequently, they instead give rise to contempt and ridicule toward pure practices. As Ciyun said: "Doubt is an obstacle to faith. If even mundane minor virtues cannot be accomplished, how much less so the Great Path of Bodhi?
Those who disparage the provisional vehicle do not understand that the Land of Bliss is the One Vehicle; thus, they all point to it with derision and mock its coarse practices.
Because they do not understand the fruit [of the path] and instead single out the myriad practices for promotion, they disparage and mock them. As Ciyun said:

"Some roll up their sleeves to reject them as 'lesser teachings' (Hīnayāna), while others laugh loudly and dismiss them as 'provisional vehicles' (upāya-yāna); because their words contradict the scriptures and delude people regarding the eternal canons."
Is this not to be immersed in a dilapidated house, willingly enduring eternal delusion for kalpas?

[Commentary] The four lines beginning with "Is this not" reveal the loss; the first two lines show that the attachment is profound. "Dānmiàn" (耽湎) means to be submerged or infatuated. "Xiùzhái" (朽宅), the dilapidated house, refers generally to the three realms (*tridhātu*).
Because it is attained through one's own realization and not by depending on another—as stated in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*—it is said to be "willingly endured" (*zìgān*).
Because there is no time of emergence, it is called "eternal kalpas.
To be rebellious toward one's compassionate parents brings deep pain at the total waste of a single lifetime.

[Commentary] The latter two phrases refer to the gravity of the transgression of rebellion; "rebellious" (*pèilì*) is synonymous with "to betray" or "to fail. "Compassionate parents" refers to those whom he summoned.

Because the Master of the Commentary on the "Chapter on Avalokiteśvara" and Mahāsthāmaprāpta felt such intense compassion, he said, "Deeply pained," and because [beings] live and die in vain, he said, "Wasted away.
The meaning of this section of the text does not exceed the three obstructions: the first two lines refer to the obstruction of afflictions (*kleśa-āvaraṇa*);
the next two lines refer to the obstruction of karma (*karma-āvaraṇa*); and the final four lines refer to the obstruction of retribution (*vipāka-āvaraṇa*).
One must believe that it is not by relying on other powers that one can sever karmic afflictions without end, nor is there any way to escape birth and death without encountering this gateway.

[Commentary] Among the exhortations to believe and accept, these words of encouragement are spoken because, due to the aforementioned deluded attachments, one does not believe in the pure realm. Thus, they serve as an exhortation.
This serves to clarify that one must have decisive faith in the words [of the Buddha]. Regarding "other power" (*tariki*), the *Ten Doubts Treatise* (*Jūgi-ron*) states:

"As for 'self-power,' practicing the path in this land makes it extremely difficult to attain birth in the Pure Land; it is like a lame person walking on foot, who cannot travel more than a few li in a single day and endures great hardship.
As for 'other power,' if one believes in the Vow-power of Amitābha to embrace those who practice mindfulness of the Buddha..."

When sentient beings single-mindedly cultivate the Samādhi of Buddha-remembrance (*buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*), their spiritual capacity and the Buddha’s response correspond, and they immediately attain rebirth.
This is like a person traveling by water who, by relying on the power of a boat, reaches a thousand *li* in a mere moment. This gate is the singular dharma of the Pure Land;
just as one enters or exits the mundane world through a door, this practice serves as the gateway, which can be understood by contrasting it with the three aforementioned obstacles.
"Those who hear and uphold [this teaching] are quite numerous, perfectly coinciding with the conditions of the time.

[Commentary: To express his intent in composing this work, the author first directly expresses his intention through the first two phrases. These clarify that the scriptural text accords with the spiritual capacities of the audience;

since the Sūtra says, "those who hear this sūtra and receive and uphold it," it is called "hearing and upholding" (*śrutadhara*). Since those who take pleasure in it are not just one or two, it is said they are "quite numerous."
Although their writings are numerous, few have exhausted the essential meaning.

[Commentary: The latter two phrases clarify that the various masters failed to grasp the core tenets. Since three versions—those of Cien, Gushan, and Jingjue—are currently circulating in the world, it is said they are "numerous.
Because they do not exhaust the purport of the sutra, it is said they "rarely exhaust" it.
"I exhaust the tip of my brush to provide this exposition, daring to emulate the former masters.
[Commentary] Regarding the lines following "Exhaust," the next section clarifies the composition of the treatise. The first two phrases describe the writing of the commentary;

"exhausting the tip of the brush" refers to one's calligraphy, which in turn points to one's learning and experience. The *Wenxuan* states: "One exhausts the six principles within the breast and investigates the eight styles at the tip of the brush."
Because he takes up the Dharma, it is said: "I dare to teach. "Teaching" (xiào) means learning.
He extends his tongue-mark to praise and extol, vowing to be one with all Buddhas.
[Commentary] The final two lines clarify that the purpose of extending the tongue to praise and extol while preaching is to open up and unfold the sutra through this cause.

This circulated text is identical to that of the Buddhas of the six directions below, who extend their broad and long tongues to cover the great trichiliocosm and praise Śākyamuni for preaching this difficult-to-believe Dharma.
The Great Void may have its limits, but my humble aspirations are inexhaustible; I respectfully urge those on this same vessel to deeply honor this Way.
[Commentary] At the very bottom, the *Zhuanji* (Record) cites the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*: "The nature of Śūnyatā may perish, but the *śakrābhilagna* heart does not waver.

This is a respectful exhortation, like an encouragement. "Those on the same boat" refers to those of the same path; the *Yeshu* (Exposition of Meaning) says, "Those on the same boat each examine and know this for themselves.
The *Ji* (Record) states that the boat is a metaphor for the Holy Dharma by which one may be delivered across [the sea of suffering]. The *Yijing* (Book of Changes) says, "Those on the same..."
When boats cross one another, what concern need there be for the different hearts of the Hu and Yue peoples? This path refers to the present sutra, the *Nianfo Samādhi*.

Before explaining this sutra, one must first summarize its essential principles through thematic categories; only then can the meaning and intent of the text be elucidated through its literary structure.

[Commentary] In the initial section of the general introduction, the first sentence provides a general heading. The first two sentences of the subsequent division of chapters clarify the "Exposition of the Meaning" (*yì* [義]), which consists of four gates.

The following two sentences clarify the "Explanation of the Text" (*shìwén* [釋文]), which refers to the meaning of the three divisions. Since these are the gates of the school of interpretation, they are called "gates of meaning.
The great meanings contained within the sutra do not transcend teaching, principle, practice, and fruit; yet, without the accumulation of study to penetrate the subtle, one cannot grasp them.

To exhaustively investigate the profound and fully penetrate the principles, how could one achieve such understanding? Therefore, the Master of the Commentary, prior to the actual exegesis of the text, sets forth four gates to encompass the essential purport of the Sūtra;

this is done with clarity and lucidity so that students may enter through these gates to glimpse its beauty and richness, and subsequently, when they proceed to the detailed textual analysis, they shall not lose the grand design. This "framework" (綱) is like the horizontal ropes on a net.
Now, if one grasps the main framework of these doctrinal gates, both the outline and the details will be orderly; if one enters the gates, the underlying principles will remain unimpaired.

From beginning to end, although the various teachings of the Greatly Awakened World-Honored One throughout his lifetime differ in being either Mahāyāna or Hīnayāna, they do not exceed the four categories of teaching, principle, practice, and fruition.

Teaching reveals principle, principle gives rise to practice, and through practice one attains fruition; when subsumed within these four dharmas, there is scarcely anything that is not fully encompassed.
[Commentary] In the general presentation of the thematic gates, the first two characters [“Great Awakening” (Dàjué)] mark the title and indicate the Greatly Awakened World-Honored One as the speaker;
the following two phrases indicate the teaching that is spoken; and the subsequent lines summarize the characteristics of what is expounded.

The four dharmas and their mutual dependence are self-evident within the text. Question: Now, this commentary explains the four dharmas based on the sutra; I wonder upon what textual authority it relies?

The response in terms of meaning is as follows: The texts are not of a single canon; their meanings are scattered across various compilations. To synthesize their great essence, there is nothing that exceeds this [work].

This is truly because our Buddha, in preaching the Dharma according to the capacities of sentient beings, ensured that every teaching would become a formal doctrine. His intent was for those teachings to reach the appropriate audience, who, by relying on the doctrine, would achieve understanding and recognize the principles it elucidates.
Once these principles are revealed, they must be put into practice; through such practice, there will inevitably be realization, leading to the fruit of Nirvana, which is not merely singular.

The Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time are likewise so. This is because from beginning to end, as one ascends from the state of an ordinary person to that of a sage through a single process of cultivation and realization, these four dharmas are complete and perfect, neither more nor less;

they are like the four seasons of spring, summer, autumn, and winter, or the four cardinal directions of east, south, west, and north—how could even a thousand sages appearing again in successive generations alter them? (Commentary)
The Master profoundly clarified the intent of the teachings of a single lifetime, unifying them under a single principle by establishing these four dharmas;

such a teaching is rarely heard of in antiquity or the present, and only those of great realization and broad vision can understand it—those with narrow perspectives are not fit to deliberate upon it.

For instance, the Tiantai system of the five periods and eight teachings, along with its five levels of profound meaning, is likewise a comprehensive mastery of the sūtras and śāstras that exhaustively investigates the transformative power of the Buddha’s intent.
Originating from the sacred mind, these were established to form the rules and regulations of a single school; they function spontaneously in harmony with the *sūtras*.
How could one seek their source by means of mere fragments of text or isolated points of doctrine?

The great predecessors of old extensively propagated and elucidated the gates of the teaching, despite their myriad differences, solely because the Buddha’s intent is perfectly integrated while its application to sentient beings varies according to their capacities.

Since one acts with sovereign mastery both vertically and horizontally, there is nothing that cannot be accomplished; how could this be merely a matter of eccentricity? In the *Chaoxuan ji* (Record of Transcending the Mysterious), it is asked:

"Now, regarding the four dharmas in this commentary, must they have a scriptural basis? The answer is: "They are based on the sūtras. [The questioner asks: "If so, which sūtra is it? The answer is: "It is the Teaching itself (*jiao*). The Teaching exists to manifest principle (*li*);

relying on principle, one gives rise to practice (*xing*); when practice is perfected, one attains the fruit (*guo*). These four dharmas follow one another in sequence; they do not depend [on anything else]."
How can you now claim that this explanation is utterly groundless? Since you say it is based on the sūtras, you ought to point out the specific scriptural passages to inspire faith in others.
As there is no definitive basis, where is the evidence from the sūtras? Not only is your answer inappropriate to the question, but your previous objection remains unresolved.
The *Yuánxiū jì* also states: "The four dharmas encompass the sūtras; what further purpose would there be?"

According to the *Fourfold Identity* (*Sishiyi*), it clarifies that the scriptures of both China and India follow the same track, extending even to the teachings of Guangzhai, which speak of one person, one cause, one fruit;

and the Tiantai principles, which speak of one practice, one teaching, one person, and so forth. Now, I maintain that this explanation fails to recognize the intent behind the transformation [of beings].
The "fourfold identity" in other schools is strictly limited to the *Lotus Sūtra*; only when the provisional is opened and the real is revealed can one truly discuss it.
In the past, before the assembly had even convened, how could one so hastily employ a name based on circumstances that distorts the reality and invites derision from others?
The erroneous claims in the two records are numerous and inconsistent; I cannot refute them all in detail, but let scholars examine them for themselves.
The general outline of the initial exposition of the teachings consists of two parts: first, clarifying the arising of the teachings; second, distinguishing the characteristics of the teachings.

[Commentary] Regarding the first section, which provides a general clarification of the arising of the teachings, the former scholars said: "To follow one's nature is called the Way (dharma); to cultivate the Way is called the teaching (śāsana).
This is because sentient beings inherently possess the nature of awakening and are all capable of reaching the Way; however, due to external objects...

As beings transmigrate and forget change, they must rely upon verbal teachings as a support and aid; therefore, when a Buddha appears in the world, he speaks where there is nothing to say, meeting the capacities and conditions of sentient beings so that they may cultivate the path according to the teachings, realize their nature, and attain Buddhahood.

Thus, one knows that the merit of the Dharma-teachings in benefiting all things is vast. As for why there are both general and specific [teachings], the general refers to the overall intent behind the establishment of the teachings. No...

It is not for the sake of causing sentient beings to open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision that one separately investigates the differences in the practices clarified by the teachings on dependent origination;
rather, these are distinct because they are tailored to the specific capacities of those who cultivate and advance upon them.

The *Zhongbenqi jing* states: The Buddha said, "The Tathāgata, out of immeasurable great compassion and pity for the three realms, has appeared in the world to brilliantly expound the Way and its teachings, so that all sentient beings may universally obtain their share of the Dharma's benefits.
He reveals and shows the five destinies to deliver those not yet delivered, and he decisively clarifies the path of birth-and-death and nirvāṇa."
[Commentary] The term "Great Text" (*dàběn*) refers to the two-fascicle *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra* translated by Saṃghavarman of the Cao Wei dynasty;
compared to the current single-fascicle version, it is called the "Small Text. This [Great Text] consists of two sections:

from the beginning up to "the benefit of the Dharma" constitutes the upper fascicle, while from "opening" down to "the Way" constitutes the lower fascicle. The two characters "The Buddha said" (*fó yán*) are the words of the scribe (the *jīngjiā*).
The Tathāgata points out that the immeasurable great compassion of Śākyamuni is precisely the Buddha-mind; his pity for the three realms is his commiseration for sentient beings.

The two lines following "that which is bestowed" constitute the establishment of the teaching, while the two lines following "universally" constitute its application to those with the capacity [for enlightenment].
As the *Caryāpraṇidhāna-parivarta* states: "Because all Buddhas and Tathāgatas take great compassion as their essence," it is due to the multitudes of sentient beings.
The arising of the bodhicitta is the cause, and through the bodhicitta one achieves equal and perfect enlightenment;

this is the compassion of identical essence (*sābhinnasvabhāva-karuṇā*), which universally encompasses the realm of all sentient beings. Because the objects [of this compassion] are infinite, great compassion is likewise infinite.

In the sutras, it is intended to clarify that the Buddha and sentient beings are non-dual, sharing the same source of awakening, and that they perfectly illumine all phenomena; thus have all Buddhas realized it.

The fundamental intent is to give rise to compassion for sentient beings who, being deluded, are powerfully subjected to various illusory sufferings; because this compassion can extract them from suffering, it is specifically mentioned.

Alternatively, some say that [the text] merely cites one of the four immeasurables, but this is by no means the meaning of the passage. The three realms belong to the "retributive environment" (*niśraya-vipāka*);
here, the environment is used to manifest the primary reality. This is truly because sentient beings, since beginningless time, have been attached to and clinging within the three realms.
The suffering of birth and death has no time of liberation; therefore, the Tathāgata gives rise to a compassionate mind and appears in the world to rescue and deliver beings.
As the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says: "For the sake of these sentient beings, he gives rise to the great compassionate mind. The Patriarch’s Preface states:
"With great pity and vast salvation, he pulls out those submerged in the flowing current; with a singular heart of compassion, he rescues the ignorant."
"Delusion" refers to the loss of one's true nature; "arising" means the manifestation of responsive transformation (*nirmāṇa*).

"Worlds" refers to the mundane world, specifically indicating the three thousandfold world system (*trisāhasramahāsāhasralokadhātu*) in its proximate sense, and extending to the entire *dharmadhātu* in its remote sense—namely, the three types of worlds consisting of sentient beings, the receptacle world, and the five aggregates.

"To illuminate and expound" means that "illumination" is to make manifest, while "expounding" is to propagate; by relying on the teachings to establish practice, one is able to approach the noble paths of the three vehicles.
It is said that in the Way of the Dao, when plants and trees first split their husks, they are called "sprouts" (*meng*); this term signifies abundance.

When the conditions and opportunities for the Dao-mind first arise, it is likewise like a sprout; therefore, this analogy is employed. "Obtaining benefit" means receiving spiritual advantage. The Master said:

"The term 'benefit for the multitude of sprouts' (*qunmeng falì*) is still somewhat general and diffuse; therefore, I cite the five destinies to clarify the decision regarding those who have not yet been delivered."

The text of the latter fascicle states: "Proclaiming the Way of the Teachings, severing the net of all doubts, uprooting the foundation of craving and desire, and blocking the source of all evils—illuminating them with such clarity as to be perfectly distinct.
This connects to the present text’s phrases regarding "opening and revealing" and so forth. "Delivering those not yet delivered" refers to the Four Great Vows;
as for the statement "Sentient beings are boundless, I vow to deliver them," this refers to the four [vows] of one's own practice.
The Four Great Vows for Transforming Others state: "Those who have not yet crossed over, may they cross over; those who have not yet been liberated, may they be liberated;
those who have not yet found peace, may they find peace; those who have not yet attained *nirvāṇa*, may they attain *nirvāṇa*.

*Nirvāṇa* is a corruption and transformation of the Sanskrit term, translated as "extinction" (*mie*) and "crossing over" (*du*). As for the term "decisive correctness," it is because birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) and *nirvāṇa* are fundamentally non-dual.
If one is deluded regarding the Dharma, nirvana is itself birth-and-death; if one awakens to it, birth-and-death is itself nirvana.
Sentient beings, through false views, mistakenly identify nirvana as birth-and-death; I now provide this definitive resolution so that they may return to the correct path.
This clarifies that the great intent of the supramundane teachings encompasses all scriptures; this is what is called the general explanation of the emergence of the teaching.
[Commentary] The conclusion and its manifestation are evident.
Next, based on the present sutra, the five intents will be briefly stated.
[Commentary] To specifically distinguish the general and particular aspects of equanimity, we shall now seek the underlying intent of this sutra by focusing on its specific application.

First, because [the Buddha] wishes to cause sentient beings to know the suffering of the Sahā world and to seek liberation from it, the sutra states: "The sentient beings in that land have no manifold sufferings."
[Commentary] First, the main text clearly explains this; below, it concludes by manifesting that the initial stage is the aversion to suffering.

Second, in order to cause [beings] to know the Buddha’s realm and give rise to longing and admiration, the following section clarifies the adornments of the environment and its inhabitants, exhorting them to be born in that land.
[Commentary] The second [aspect] is the joyful aspiration.
The third is that which causes the mind to be gathered and dwell securely in the *nien-fo samādhi* (Buddha-recollection samādhi); thus, it says below:
"Upon hearing the teaching of Amitābha Buddha, one upholds his name with single-mindedness and without distraction," and so forth.
[Commentary] Three refers to the arising of practice.

Four refers to causing the destruction of hindrances, liberation from suffering, and the attainment of pure bliss; therefore, it is said below that "when such a person’s life ends, their mind is not inverted, and they immediately attain rebirth," and so forth.
[Commentary] The fourth is receiving birth [in that land].
The fifth is causing one to be born in that land so as to achieve enlightenment; hence it is said below: "All these people shall attain non-retrogression," and so forth.
[Commentary] These five [stages] constitute the path of realization; however, this sequence of five meanings proceeds from the shallow to the profound as a matter of natural principle.
This clarifies that the primary intent of the sutra’s exposition is confined to the present text, which is what is called the "separate narration of the arising of the teaching."

Next, we shall distinguish the characteristics of the teaching. The teachings on the Pure Land and the contemplations therein universally clarify that the Buddhas of the ten directions in the present exist;

this is evidenced by the passage cited below regarding the Buddhas of the six directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, who extend their broad and long tongues to exhort faith in this sutra.

Furthermore, according to the text below, if good men and good women hear and uphold this sutra, they will all attain non-retrogression from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* without passing through gradual stages.

*Bodhi*. [Commentary] Next, in the section distinguishing the characteristics of the teaching (*śāsana-lakṣaṇa*), "teaching" refers generally to the Dharma spoken by the Tathāgata through his four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) and eightfold voice (*aṣṭāṅga-svara*);

"characteristic," however, specifically designates the modes of practice (*pratipatti-lakṣaṇa*) expounded within that teaching, which differ according to the Great or Small Vehicles. "Characteristic" here refers to their identity.
Because one can distinguish the characteristics of the teaching school by examining its formal features, it is called the "characteristics of the teaching" (*jiaoxiang*).

Since this section first correctly elucidates [the teaching], the subsequent conclusion clarifies the reason for citing the various Buddhas as proof at the beginning. This is because in the Lesser Vehicle there is no mention of other Buddhas, whereas in the Greater Vehicle there are teachings regarding Buddhas as numerous as the atoms of all lands;
since this sutra discusses the Buddhas of the worlds of the ten directions, as many as the sands of the Ganges River...
The Buddha’s verified teaching confirms that this contemplation is not partial or limited to the Small Vehicle.
Furthermore, by citing those who hear and uphold [the Dharma] and attain non-retrogression in Bodhi, it is proven that since their realization is already vast, its meaning becomes even more manifest.

As for the statement that one does not pass through gradual stages, those born in that land all universally arouse the Great Mind and suddenly cultivate Great Practices, never again falling back as they are destined to realize Bodhi; this is unlike the situation in this land.
Because Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas attain their minor fruits through gradual cultivation and progress, it is said that they do not "pass through" [the stages].
Thus, one should know that all teaching gates of the Pure Lands are the Dharma of the Great Vehicle’s perfect and sudden attainment of Buddhahood;
they are certainly not partial or small-vehicle teachings, as is discussed in detail elsewhere.
[Commentary] As explained in detail elsewhere in the *Jianjing shu* (Commentary on the Contemplation Sutra), there are two parts to the clarification of principle (*li*).
Principle is the essence of the teaching (*jiaoti*), which is also divided into two: first, the general, and second, the specific.

[Commentary] Regarding the second part, the clarification of principle: within the section marking the divisions, "principle is the essence of the teaching" means that principle is the name for emptiness and quiescence, and its essence is...
Taking the primary substance as the meaning, that which is non-dual is made dual; though momentarily divided into two names, it is non-dual in its principle and essence, being as one.
Since the teaching is established according to the principle, the teaching itself constitutes the essence.
From beginning to end, all Mahāyāna teachings take the *vaipulya* (extensive) reality-mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) as their essence.

[Commentary] Generally speaking, the first two phrases of the middle section establish the name; the term "all" excludes only the Deer Park [teachings], while universally encompassing the entire period of the Buddha’s life, none of which is not Mahāyāna.
"Method" (fang) refers to the Vaipulya and other [Mahāyāna] teachings;
these are "equal" (pingdeng). [Commentary]: The section below "method" restates and explains the first part. It explains the two characters "fang" and "deng.

Because the wondrous principle of true reality (bhūtatathatā) extends horizontally across all phenomena, it is called "vaipulya" (broad); because it vertically encompasses both ordinary beings and sages, it is called "equal."

[Commentary] The following section provides the formal explanation of the essence and characteristics (*tattva-lakṣaṇa*). First, it is shown through the horizontal and vertical dimensions that [the reality] is all-pervasive. As the Sūtra says:
"Only Buddhas and Buddhas can exhaustively fathom the true aspect (*bhūta-lakṣaṇa*) of all dharmas. What is called the "true aspect" is precisely the profound and inconceivable realm;
because it is real and not false, it is termed the "true aspect. The *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra* states: "All dharmas..."
From the very beginning, it is free from the characteristics of verbal expression, free from the characteristics of names and words, and free from the characteristics of mental objects;
it is ultimately equal, without change or variation, and indestructible. It is solely this one mind, and is therefore called *tathatā* (Suchness).
*Tathatā* is simply another name for the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). Furthermore, this true mark is not separate from all phenomena; every phenomenon accords with the truth.
Because it takes reality as its characteristic by means of the ultimate wondrous principle, it is called the "Reality-mark" (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
Its essence is lofty and vast, encompassing the *dharmadhātu*; because Vairocana pervades all places, it is said to extend horizontally across all phenomena.

Because it penetrates the three periods of time, exhausting the abyss and reaching the source, such that reality is found within every particular thing and nothing is not the Middle Way, it is said to encompass vertically both the ordinary and the sagely. Thus one should know.
The true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) encompasses all horizontal and vertical dharma-gates; since there is not a single dharma that is not true reality, it is said:
"Except for the true reality of all dharmas, everything else is the work of Māra. "Horizontal" refers to all phenomena, while "vertical" refers to the ordinary and the sage;

these are merely distinguished as horizontal and vertical, though their textual expressions vary. Where there is the horizontal, there is the vertical; where there is the vertical, there is the horizontal—they cannot be pursued separately.
One forms a substantial understanding based on mere names;
therefore, one should know that all phenomena, whether horizontal or vertical, are entirely born of their own conditions, are all inconceivable, and none are not the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).

[Commentary] The phrase "therefore, next" indicates that all phenomena are themselves the true mark, fearing that those who have not yet understood might think that the true mark exists apart from all phenomena.
Because there is a separate reality (dharmatā), it is pointed out that all phenomena—whether horizontal or vertical—are dependently originated.
When these phenomena arise, they come from nowhere; therefore, they are called "unborn. When these phenomena perish, they go nowhere; therefore, they are called "unperishing.
How could they be subject to conceptual thought? This inconceivable realm is precisely the reality (dharmatā).
This encompasses the principles elucidated throughout the Mahāyāna teachings of a single lifetime.
[Commentary] The following section concludes and clarifies the meaning.
Regarding the distinction between the two terms:
[Commentary] In the initial section of the detailed exposition, the first phrase establishes the heading.

In this present sutra, the principle to be elucidated is precisely the inconceivable merit of the adornments of both the primary and secondary bodies (*āśraya* and *āśrita*), which are the fruits realized through Amitābha’s cultivation of causes.
[Commentary] Now, the formal thesis is established below.
It is because, within the causal stage, one gives rise to great vows of signlessness and cultivates wondrous practices of non-abiding, thereby eliciting the holy fruit of non-attainment;
since phenomena and the wondrous principle are interfused such that form is non-form, the bodies and lands thus elicited are none other than the true mark (dharmatā).
[Commentary] "Ultimately" means to investigate thoroughly.
This refers to what the Sūtra says: "As I now praise the inconceivable merit of Amitābha Buddha.
[Commentary] This citation of "inconceivable merit" as proof refers to the wondrous principle of the true reality (*bhūtatathatā*), and for the time being, it is discussed in this manner.

Because Amitābha’s practice is both cultivation and manifestation, it can be described as having distinct causes and effects; yet, there is not a single thing among his environment and inhabitants that is not a dharma produced through conditioned arising with effort.

How then could these be the realized principle? In investigating Amitābha’s causal-ground practice, realization, vows, and conduct, all three are non-conforming-to-nature (non-conceptual) and entirely without effortful action.
His environment and inhabitants, as well as his body and lands, are all in perfect accord with the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
Based on this, the essential body of the present sutra is established; by citing the text of the subsequent sutra, the three preceding meanings are proven to correspond perfectly.
If it were not a sublime principle, how could it be called "inconceivable"?
[Commentary] If one were to counter-argue from below:
regarding the "practice of the three knowledges" (*traividya*), the practice itself constitutes the doctrinal system (*śāstra*). This system also possesses both general and specific aspects.

[Commentary] Within the initial section on the practice of the three knowledges, the phrase "the practice itself constitutes the doctrinal system" indicates that the system refers to what is contained within a single sutra.
The essential point of exposition is that practice arises based on the school; thus, what is called the "school" is not necessarily practice, whereas what is called "practice" must be the school.
First, it is generally explained that great practice does not go beyond the arousal of the mind for supreme enlightenment and the cultivation of the six perfections and myriad practices.
These are fully contained within the various sutras and are not cited here in detail.

[Commentary] Among the four lines, the first two correctly demonstrate the Middle Way, while the latter two point to the extensive teachings. The "unsurpassed mind of the Way" (*anuttara-mārga-citta*) is the great mind of *bodhi*;
the "six perfections and myriad practices" are the great conduct of Samantabhadra. "To arouse" means to bring forth and develop.
Sentient beings inherently possess the three causes of Buddha-nature; because they are deluded regarding this principle, ignorance serves as the condition for the arising of sentient beings.
Those who awaken to this principle take the teachings and practice as conditions for the arising of perfect enlightenment.

Now, by taking the teachings and practice as conditions, one awakens in a single thought-moment and the three causes all manifest together—this is what is meant by "the seed of the Buddha arises from conditions."
Second, regarding those who advocate for specific [practices], the cultivation of pure karma to attain rebirth in a Pure Land is a distinct gateway and a specialized path for transcendence.
[Commentary] Regarding the first section of the "Specific Exposition," the phrase "a distinct gateway" refers to the *Guanjing shu* (Commentary on the Contemplation Sutra), which states:

"The holy teachings expounded throughout Śākyamuni’s single transformation [of the world] generally consist of two types: first, the Way of entering the teaching via the Sahā world; second, the Pure Land."
The teachings on rebirth in the Pure Land are all clearly explained as they were categorized in that commentary (*shū*).
Within the practices for pure karma, there are furthermore many varieties, as the methods of practice shown in various sutras each differ.
[Commentary] In the initial section distinguishing these differences, seven sutras are cited to demonstrate their distinct characteristics.
The *Contemplation Sūtra* describes the three kinds of merit and wondrous contemplations;
the *Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* prescribes hanging silk banners and canopies for one day and night, or observing the precepts and maintaining the fast for ten days and ten nights;
and the *Mahākaruṇā Sūtra* teaches reciting the name for a single day while exhorting others to do the same.
In the *Pratyutpanna Sūtra*, it is said that for one day, if one maintains mindfulness before them, one shall remain constantly without sitting or lying down for ninety days.
In the *Dharmaghoṣa Sūtra*, it is said that for ten days and ten nights, one should perform prostrations and mindfulness during the six periods.
The *Dhāraṇī-saṃgraha* recites various divine mantras, while the *Mahādharma-dundubhi-sūtra* merely requires one to form the intention of knowing that the Buddha exists.
These skillful means respond to capacities through diverse methods of practice; though the teaching gates differ, there are none that do not lead to rebirth [in the Pure Land].

Now, this sutra specifically demonstrates the method of holding the Name; as this is precisely the core tenet of the sutra and is essential for the present time, it must be explained in detail and cannot be treated in a general or superficial manner.

[Commentary] Second, regarding the section on "expedient means" and below, one investigates the Buddha’s intention: though the paths differ, they return to the same destination. Within this sutra, the first part definitively demonstrates the core of the teaching.
