[Commentary] The name "Awakened One" is general; this specific term refers to one of the ten titles of the ultimate fruit of wondrous awakening (*miaojué jìngjiù jíguǒ*).
Thus, it is a general title. [Record] Since the name "Awakened One" is used for other [levels], this is called a general title to distinguish it from such overlap.
"At Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park. [Commentary on the *Śū*]:
Regarding "At Śrāvastī" and so forth, this indicates the location where the sutra was preached. [Recorded Notes on the *Jì*]: Among these five [points], the first is a general indication.
[Commentary] To cite Śrāvastī is to indicate the sphere of his wandering and teaching; to cite Jetavana is to indicate the place where he resided—thus, the location is established.
[Record] Next, the specific explanation cites the kingdom so that those from afar may hear of it, and cites the garden so that those nearby may know of it.
[Commentary]: Śrāvastī is translated as "Renowned for Wealth" (Wénwù), because its abundance of people and goods was far-famed throughout all lands.
[Commentary]: It is named after Jeta, who donated the trees, and Anāthapiṇḍada, who purchased the grove, together establishing this Buddha-field.

[Commentary: Regarding the sixth [section], "Together with the great bhikṣus," it indicates that he was assembled with the fourfold assembly of both monastics and laypeople, and did not hear this alone;
thus, the assembly is perfected. [Record: Among these six points, this briefly shows that Ānanda further cites the testimony of the assembly to prove that [the teaching] is not false.
Since the "fourfold assembly" refers to both monastics and laypeople, they consist of monks, nuns, men, and women, rather than humans, devas, nāgas, or ghosts.
[Commentary] There are three categories of assemblies: first, the assembly of śrāvakas; second, the assembly of bodhisattvas (the "and all those below" refers to this);
third, the assembly of humans and devas (beginning with Śakra Devendra). [Record] In the detailed explanation of the general classification, the first section is divided into these three categories.
[Commentary: Because the Śrāvakas constantly attend upon the Buddha and their deportment is even more sublime, they are placed at the front.

Because Bodhisattvas appear and disappear without fixed form or dress and are not restricted by such conventions, they follow next. Because the worldly multitudes of devas and humans differ entirely in form and dress, they are listed last.
[Record: Next, regarding the sequence of before and after: because Śrāvakas act as shadows and echoes wherever they are, they are always in attendance as renunciants.
Because they possess the [thirty-two] marks, their deportment is superior; because they practice for themselves and transform others, they have no fixed status as either lay or ordained;

and because they do not restrict themselves to the forms or secular dress of humans or devas, they are said to be entirely distinct [from them]. This classification of the sequence is based on external appearances.
Guishan, however, maintained that śrāvakas sink into emptiness, those of the human and heavenly realms cling to existence, and bodhisattvas abide in the Middle Way.
They are listed between the positions of the youngest and the eldest to represent this.
[Commentary] Regarding the first section, there are four parts: first, indicating the number; second, praising the virtues of both groups; third, listing the names of the elders and others;
fourth, summarizing with "In this way," etc. △ Regarding the first part.
[He was] together with a great assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus.

[Commentary on the Sub-commentary]: Regarding "great bhikṣus," this refers to the foremost disciples such as those listed below; the other attendant disciples, numbering one thousand two hundred and so forth, are not individually enumerated.
[Sub-commentary on the Record]: In the general exposition following the explanation of the Śrāvakas, the section first distinguishes between the Great and the Small Vehicles.
[Commentary] *Bhikṣu* is sometimes called *bhikṣu*; this is translated as "mendicant" (*qǐshì*). He begs for food to sustain his body and begs for the Dharma to refine his mind.

It is also translated as "Terrifier of Māras," meaning that his resolve terrifies those Māras and his virtues cause the Māras to fear him. It is also said he "destroys evil": by receiving the precepts, he destroys karma; through concentration and wisdom, he destroys delusions.
These three are names based on causes, while the title [of Bhikṣu] is based on the result, as explained later. [Record] Next, the name based on the cause is translated as "mendicant."

The *śrāmaṇera* follows [the path] through conduct; the *bhikṣu* follows it through his resolve; the *prahāṇika* (one who destroys evil) follows it through his merit; and those who cultivate precepts, concentration, and wisdom follow it by destroying delusion, karma, and suffering.

[Sū] *Saṃgha*, when fully expressed, is *saṃgha*; this translates as "assembly. From four or more individuals upward, they preside over all *karmavācanā* rites that extinguish evil and give rise to good.
Because these matters generally encompass both ordinary beings and sages, and universally include all phenomena and principles, it is called an "assembly" (*zhòng*). [Jì]

*Saṃgha* is translated as "the assembly" (*zhòng*). While the term "assembly" is general, here it specifically refers to the four types of individuals at the initial stage, who are provisionally taken as its essence.

It is the great means for extinguishing evil; one must not regard it with pride. Rebirth is the ultimate point for the cultivation of goodness, and nothing surpasses receiving this essence. The five stages of mental abiding (*pañca-vasthāna-citta-sthiti*) and the collective and specific contemplations are called the "external ordinary beings" (*bāhya-pṛthagjana*).
The stages of *uṣmagata*, *kṣānti*, and *mūrdhan* are the foremost among the world and are called the "internal ordinary beings" (*adhyātma-pṛthagjana*). This concludes the summary.

The two types of ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*), together with those on the preparatory stages (*tāvat-bhūmi*), are collectively termed "ordinary monks" (*prthag-bhikṣu*). From the first fruit (*srotāpanna*) up to the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), they are collectively termed "noble monks" (*ārya-bhikṣu*).

Furthermore, those from the first fruit upward who are still in training (*śaikṣa*) or have attained no-more-learning and have realized the principle of the True Dharma (*satya-dharma*) are called the "Sangha of Harmony in Principle" (*li-he seng*).

Those whose body, speech, and mind are unified, and whose precepts, views, and livelihoods are equal and uniform, are called the "Sangha of Harmony in Practice" (*shi-he seng*). These encompass the various meanings mentioned above.
[The text] concludes by indicating the names of the assembly.
[Commentary]: When the Buddha first attained enlightenment, he converted the three Kāśyapas along with their combined disciples of one thousand people;

subsequently, he converted Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana along with their combined disciples of two hundred and fifty people. All of these were originally followers of external paths who encountered [the Buddha].

Because the Buddha attained deliverance and his grace was profound, [Kāśyapa] constantly attended upon him. [Commentary] Within the section providing specific details, this subsection explains the general number of the master and disciples mentioned in the sutra and the reason for their extensive listing.
As for the "Three Kāśyapas," they were the three brothers Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa, Gayā-Kāśyapa, and Nadī-Kāśyapa;
originally practitioners of fire-worship, they were converted by the Buddha and came to see the Great Master.
In the *Benqi jing* (Sutra on the Original Events), it is recorded that Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, while still practitioners of external paths, made a covenant with one another, saying:
"If we should attain the nectar of immortality, we must surely share its flavor. Later, Śāriputra first beheld the dignified and composed deportment of Aśvajit.
He then asked, "Who is your teacher? What Dharma do you preach? According to the *Wufen lü* (Five-Part Vinaya), Aśvajit replied: "Dharmas arise from conditions..."
"Dependent on conditions, all phenomena are empty and without a master. Another passage says: "All phenomena arise from causes and conditions, and they also cease through causes and conditions.
My Buddha, the Great Śramaṇa, constantly makes such declarations. Upon hearing this once, Śāriputra immediately realized the first fruit [of the path].
Subsequently, he transmitted it to Maudgalyāyana, who also realized the first fruit. For a long time, they had both followed non-Buddhist paths and possessed nothing at all.
Because those who have attained entry into the Buddha-dharma immediately obtain the supreme fruits, their debt of gratitude is profound.

[Commentary: Some say that because they are honored for being the first to take refuge in the Buddha, they are listed frequently; it does not necessarily mean they were always present at the assemblies.

[Commentary]: Or, as stated in the *Puyao jing* (Lalitavistara-sūtra), it is for the purpose of perfect cultivation; as cited in the *Fodi lun* (Buddhabhūmi-śāstra), there are six meanings regarding the śrāvaka:
first, to constantly attend upon the Buddha; second, to have a form similar to the Buddha; third, to be an internal retinue;
fourth, to cause bodhisattvas to give rise to reverence; fifth, to cause those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) to give rise to reverence; and sixth, for the sake of the śrāvakas themselves.

Because they harbored doubts regarding the Mahāyāna teachings, thinking they were not the Buddha’s word, [the Buddha] placed them at the head of the assembly so that they might hear the Dharma repeatedly.
[Commentary]: Within the section praising their virtues, it says:
"They are all great Arhats, well-known to the assembly."
[Commentary] The Arhat also has three translations. First, "Worthy of Offerings" (Arhat), meaning one who is capable of being a sustenance for sentient beings;
this is the fruit of the *bhikṣu* (mendicant). Second, "Slayer of Thieves," meaning one who has crushed and subdued the demonic enemies; this is the fruit of "Frightening the Māras.

Third, "Non-arising," meaning that the fetters are exhausted and suffering has vanished; this is the fruit of "Destroying Evil. [Record] Among the praises of his virtues, this is the first translation of the Sanskrit term.
[Commentary]: This means that within the assemblies listed below, the preeminent multitudes of devas and humans recognize his virtuous deeds and know his appearance;
therefore, he is called "one known by the multitude" (*saṃjñāta*). [Sub-commentary]: The following section further explains "one known by the multitude. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:
"One who can preach the dharmas of emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, non-arising, and non-cessation, as well as the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), causing people to rejoice..."
"Those who are joyful, faithful, and delighted are called *kalyāṇamitra* (spiritual friends).
[Commentary] Among those listed by name are:
the Elder Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Mahākāśyapa, and Mahākātyāyana.
Khaṇḍadravya, Revata, Cūḍapanthaka, Nanda, Ānanda, Rāhula, Gavāmpati,
Piṇḍola-Bharadvāja, Kālodāyin, Mahākapphiṇa, Bakula, and Aniruddha.

[Commentary: Because his virtue is weighty and his seniority is high, he is called an "Elder" (*sthavira*). While the term is restricted in its application to the first person [in the list], its meaning encompasses all ranks.

[Record: Among the enumeration of names, the initial explanation of the general title is as follows: because his virtue is weighty, he is "long" (*sthavira*); because his years are high, he is "old" (*vṛddha*).
[Commentary]: Śāriputra is translated here as "Son of the Body" (Shenzi) and also as "Pearl" (Zhubi). His mother possessed a beautiful form and was exceptionally intelligent;
while he was still in her eye-like pearl [in the womb], people, honoring the mother through the excellence of the child, gave him this name.
[Commentary] It is further stated that "Śā" indicates the father and "ri" indicates the mother; because both parents are manifested, it is called Śāriputra, where "Putra" means son.
[Record] The explanation of the individual components below the term "Śā" is understandable.
[Commentary]: Regarding Mahāmaudgalyāyana, "Mahā" is translated as "Great. When a name is augmented by the character "Great," all subsequent instances are to be understood analogously.
[Record]: Among the various translations for Maudgalyāyana, "Mahā" was initially employed to exclude redundancy.
[Commentary]: In the *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-sūtra*, Maudgalyāyana translates *mūlaka* as "radish" (reading *lai fu* as *luobo*).
Paramārtha states that *mudgara* translates as "pea. Because ancient seers were fond of these two things, they named their clans after them.
[Commentary] The name *Nyagrodha* is the name of a tree; because his parents prayed to the deity of this tree and thereby obtained a son, they named him after it.
[Record] Next, the personal name is translated as *Nyagrodha*, which means "white poplar."
[Commentary] Kāśyapa is translated here as "Great Tortoise Clan" (Mahākauravya). His ancestors practiced the Way, and a numinous tortoise bore the immortal scriptures in response to their virtue;
thus, they took that as the mandate for their clan name. [Record] This is the primary, direct translation for Kāśyapa.
[Commentary] Paramārtha translated it as "Light-Wave" (Jyotiprabha). This refers to the bodily radiance of an ancient seer that surged like flames, appearing as if waves were burning;
it is also called "Drinking-Light" (Pītabhāsa), so named because it can reflect other lights and cause them to disappear.

It is also the name of a tree, as [the Buddha] attained [enlightenment] by praying at this tree. [Record] Below "Paramārtha," he cites an alternative translation: *pi-p'o-lo* (Bibhela) means "Highly Manifest" (Ucchrita).
[Commentary]: Kātyāyana is translated as "Adorned Text" (*wen-shi*) and also as "Hanging Shoulders" (*jian-chui*) or "Beautiful Shoulders.
He is also named Kāla; this is translated as "Superior Thought" (*si-sheng*). Both names are derived from his clan name. [Record]:
Among the translations for Kātyāyana, the initial name is also called Kāla, which is a corruption of the Sanskrit sound.
[Commentary]: *Kauṣṭhila* is translated here as "Great Knees" (some say it is because his kneecaps were large).

[Commentary]: Śāriputra’s maternal uncle would always defeat his sister in their debates on the Dharma. When she became pregnant and could no longer defeat him, he realized she was carrying a person of wisdom.
He subsequently went to South India to recite and study various sūtras, having no leisure even to trim his nails; thus, people of the time called him "The Long-Nailed One."
The Brahmin Nakhaka. [Commentary: Regarding the phrase "as stated in the sub-commentary on Kauṣṭhila," it refers to what is seen in Guishan’s *Shu*:
that the recitation of various scriptures refers to the eighteen kinds of Vedic texts belonging to the non-Buddhist outsiders.
[Commentary: Revata is also named Revata; this is translated as "Constellation" (Skt. *nakṣatra*) or "Room/Chamber" (Skt. *śi*).
His parents obtained him by praying to a star, and thus he was named after that star.
[Commentary: Or it is said he is "Provisionally Assembled. The *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-sūtra* calls him "Ever-Making-Sound" (*Nitya-ghoṣa*). [Record: Within the section on Revata...
First, the correct translation.

[Commentary]: Someone cites the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* regarding two ghosts disputing over a corpse in an empty pavilion overnight; based on the actual facts, it was judged that they should return to the smaller ghost.
The larger ghost became enraged and tore off its hands and feet, whereupon the smaller ghost took the corpse to replace them. This was due to its afflictions (*kleśa*).
Not knowing whose body it was, he spoke of it as a "provisional combination. Furthermore, harboring doubts in his heart, he questioned everyone he met, asking, "Have you seen my body?
The monks replied, "Your body was originally the remains of another; it is not yours.
Thereupon, he attained the Way, and thus this became his name. [Commentary] This citation from the treatise provides dual proof for the latter two points.
[Commentary]: Cūḍapanthaka is translated here as "Snake-Slave" (Serpent-Servant).
Alternatively, *Cūḍa* is said to mean "by the side of the great road," and *Panthaka* means "by the side of the small road. He was given this name because he was born by the roadside. [Record]:

Regarding "Cūḍa," the *Abhidharma-nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states that there was the daughter of a householder who had an illicit affair with a slave. They fled to another country, and after a long time, she became pregnant.
He thought of returning to his native country, but gave birth midway; thus he acquired the name "The One Born by the Roadside" (Mārgaśīrṣa). [Commentary:
Nanda is here translated as "Good Joy" (Sukha-nandana) or "Delight" (Ānanda). Originally a cowherd, he tested the Buddha with matters concerning cattle-herding;
because he attained the Way through the joy of hearing the Dharma being preached, there is a place named "Nanda the Cowherd. Alternatively—
This refers to Bāṇaṃda in the Vinaya. [Commentary] Nanda is well known.
[Sub-commentary] Ānanda means "Joy" or "Undefiled. When King Śuddhodana heard that the Prince had attained Buddhahood, he was greatly overjoyed;
King Śuklodana reported the birth of a son, and the entire kingdom rejoiced, hence the name was given accordingly.
[Commentary] Ānanda’s sub-commentary explains the preceding name as "The Undefiled" (*araṇa*), stating that it refers to one who has perfected the practice leading to *nirvāṇa*.
It says that because he followed the Buddha into the palaces of devas, humans, and nāgas, his mind was free from any defilement of desire whenever he saw women.

[Commentary]: Rāhula is translated here as "Covering and Obstructing. As the legitimate son of the Buddha, he was subject to the retribution of past karma; because he remained in the womb for six years, he is called "Covering and Obstructing.
Paramārtha states that the original term for Rāhu is *asura*, who is capable of obstructing the sun and moon; therefore, it should specifically be said that he "obstructs the moon."

The Buddha said, "My Dharma is like the moon; this child obstructs me from leaving the household life immediately. Because he will be able to renounce [the world] in lifetime after lifetime, he is called 'the Obstructor' (Rāhula).
[Commentary]: Rāhula is the primary and legitimate son. First, it clarifies that he obstructs his own truth; below, it clarifies that he obstructs the Buddha’s fulfillment of past karma.
The *Benqijing* (Sūtra on the Origin of Actions) states: "In the past, when the Buddha was a king, a certain seer violated the king's prohibitions."

For six days he did not provide him with food, yet without harboring any ill will; subsequently, he fell into hell for sixty thousand years, and in his final body, he again repaid the suffering of those six years of asceticism.
Because the Prince had rejoiced in [the Bodhisattva’s] practice, he remained in his mother’s womb for six years.
[Commentary: Gavāmpati is translated here as "ox-chewer" (pronounced *shī*), or alternatively as "ox-king" or "ox-track.

In five hundred previous lifetimes, he had served as an ox-king; because the residual karmic retribution was not yet exhausted, he would constantly chew with a rumbling sound, leading people to call him "ox-chewer.
It was also for this reason that he was named "ox-track. To avoid being seen and ridiculed by others, he frequently resided in the heavens.

[Commentary]: Regarding "Kauṇḍinya": the first character is pronounced with the *zhā* rhyme (from 唼) and the *zǐ* rhyme (from 子), while the second character is pronounced with the *jiào* rhyme (from 嚼) and the *cái* rhyme (from 才).

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that because he stole others' grain ears in a previous life to observe whether they were ripe or unripe, he suffered the retribution of being born as an ox for five hundred lifetimes.

According to the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*, because he treated śramaṇas with contempt and mockery in past kalpas, he has suffered from the ailment of ruminating (*go-mukha*) in every birth and lifetime; this is explained in the *Vibhaṅga-guṇa* [section].
The *Śāstra* says: "Fearing that people might mock him and thereby incur sin, the Buddha commanded him to remain constantly in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven" (and so forth).
[Commentary: Piṇḍola Bharadvāja—this is based on his clan name, Piṇḍola, which translates as "Immovable" (referring to what he has realized);
Bharadvāja, according to Paramārtha, translates as "Swift," or alternatively "Sharp-facultied" or "Broad-speech" (referring to his root-nature). Vaira... [text ends]
He belongs to one of the clans within the [Sakyas'] gate. [Commentary] Regarding Piṇḍola, some say *Vetradhvaja* (or *Vetradhara*) and others say *Kundopadhānīya*;
these are variations in the Sanskrit and Indic pronunciations.
[Commentary] Kālodāyin is translated here as "Black Radiance" (Heiguang) or "Coarse Black" (Cūhe); he was named after his physical appearance.

[Record] According to the *Ekottarika Āgama*, his body was extremely black. Once, while walking for alms at night when the sky was pitch dark, he arrived at another's house just as a flash of lightning struck.
A woman of the household, who was pregnant at the time, mistook him for a black demon.
Frightened, she aborted the fetus; upon inquiry, it was discovered that this was a disciple of the Buddha who had arrived here while begging for alms.
She reviled him loudly, and consequently, the Buddha established the precept that one must not eat past midday.
[Commentary: Kapphiṇa is translated as "Housing Star" (Fángxiù); he was so named because his prayers to the stars resulted in his obtaining a son.
[Commentary: Furthermore, when he first left the household life and went to see the Buddha, it was raining at night and he stayed overnight at the house of a potter.
Another bhikṣu followed him there; the first bhikṣu pushed his straw mat over for the newcomer and sat on the bare ground.

The latter bhikṣu then preached the Dharma for him, and he suddenly attained the Way. This latter bhikṣu was none other than the Buddha himself; thus, he stayed overnight in the same room as the Buddha.
The name is derived from the place where he attained the Way. [Commentary] Kapphiṇa can be seen.

[Sub-commentary] *Bakkula* is translated here as "Good Appearance" (*śubha-rūpa*), also called "Noble Form," because his physical features were upright and handsome; thus he is called "Good Appearance.
He was one hundred and sixty years old, yet remained free from illness and untimely death. In the past, he observed the single precept of non-killing for ninety days.
His life span lasted for one kalpa without premature death because he once gave a single harītakī fruit to the Saṃgha;
his body was always free from illness, and having experienced this supreme retribution, he was named accordingly. [Commentary]: Among the *Bāpuka*, he observed the single precept of non-killing.

The *Dharmakośa-saṃgraha-śāstra* (Fu fazang zhuan) states that his biological mother died early, and his stepmother treated him with malice; once when he went to ask for a cake, she threw him into a furnace.
When his father saw him, he rescued him and asked for meat; [the son] was thrown into a cauldron, yet he could not die.
Again, by the riverbank, as he was pulling at his mother’s clothes, he was thrown into the river and swallowed by a large fish. A fisherman caught it and sold it in the marketplace;
the father happened to buy the fish, and when he cut open the belly with a knife, there was no damage whatsoever. He gave [the son] a medicinal fruit to eat, which restored him.

The *Pietongde lun* (Treatise on Additional Merits) states: "In the past, he once gave a single harītakī fruit to a sick monk; consequently, his present body is constantly free from illness and affliction.
Harītakī is the celestial name for the medicinal fruit brought from the world of the Heavenly Kings (*deva-rāja*). It exists in the world as a medicine that sustains life.
[Commentary]: Aniruddha is also called Anala or Aniruddha; these are all transcriptions of the Sanskrit sound *ṛ*.

It is translated as "Free from Poverty" (*wúpín*), also as "As One Wishes" (*rúyì*), or "Inexhaustible" (*wújié*). In the past, during a time of famine, he offered wild millet porridge to a Pratyekabuddha.
Because of the karmic fruit and retribution for this act over ninety-one kalpas, his provisions were always sufficient; thus, he was given this name. [Record]: An...
In the beginning of the *Shao tu* (The Rabbit), it is stated that the Sanskrit sounds were first produced and subsequently translated into the Chinese language; this may be examined in detail.
However, as for these disciples who, at that time, were followers of the Hīnayāna yet were able to participate in the assembly and hear the Great Dharma, the *Jing jue shu* says:

"These venerable ones were originally Mahāsattvas of the Dharmakāya who manifested their traces by being born in India to assist the Buddha’s transformative rites. Since they had already [attained realization] within the Hīnayāna...
Having attained the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), they have now arrived at the Vaipulya [sūtras] and are capable of hearing this sutra;

furthermore, the Tathāgata employs skillful means to guide them, desiring to cause them to feel shame for the Lesser Vehicle and to aspire toward the Great Vehicle. Therefore, the intent of the subsequent passage where he addresses Śāriputra lies therein.
[Commentary] In the summary:
"These and other great disciples.
[Commentary] This briefly cites sixteen principal figures; because it would be impossible to list them all exhaustively, it says "these and others. [Record]
In the summary, the initial point is briefly explained in the text. [Commentary] Nanshan says:
"Because his training followed after mine, he is called a younger brother; because his understanding arose from me, he is called a son.
[Commentary] Next, regarding the Bodhisattvas, there are three parts: first, indicating their number; second, listing their names starting with Mañjuśrī; third, as follows... [the text continues].
Summary. △ Regarding the beginning:
"Together with all the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas.

[Commentary] The term "all" (*zhū*) is used because, although those who heard the teaching were extremely numerous, only four names are cited here as a brief illustration. [Record] This indicates the number of the assembly of Bodhisattvas.
In the midst [of the assembly], the multitude was so vast that the sūtra compiler could not enumerate them all; therefore, he summarized them with the word "various" (zhū).
[Commentary] Regarding "Bodhisattva," it is an abbreviation of the Sanskrit term. The *Tiantai Jieshu* states:

*Mahā-bodhi-cittotpāda-sattva*, which is translated as "one who accomplishes sentient beings through the mind of the Great Way. [Record] Regarding the initial meaning of the Sanskrit translation: *mahā* is translated as "great" (*dà*). *Bodhi*...
*Bodhi* is translated as "Way" (*mārga*), *sattva* as "mind" (*citta*), and *sattva* as "sentient being.
[Commentary: Some say that *bodhisattva* is translated as "Awakened Sentient Being. "Awakening" refers to seeking the higher, which is wisdom (*prajñā*);

"sentient being" refers to transforming those below, which is compassion (*karuṇā*). [Record: According to the second interpretation, awakening is one's own practice; therefore, it is called "seeking the higher," which is identical [to the previous explanation].

The "upper" refers to the mind of the Great Way (*mahāyānacitta*); because sentient beings are transformed through it, it is called "transforming others below," which corresponds to the aforementioned "accomplishing sentient beings above.
[Commentary] Among the enumeration of names:
Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, Bodhisattva Ajita, Bodhisattva Gandhahastin, and Bodhisattva Nityodyukta.
[Commentary] Mañjuśrī is also called Mañjuśrī; this is translated as "Wondrous Auspiciousness" (*Miaojixiang*). "Wondrous" (*Miao*) specifically signifies...
That which is realized is auspicious; its excellence lies in benefiting sentient beings. [Commentary] Regarding the initial explanation of the name among the listed titles:

The sensation of pain gives rise to the suffering of suffering; the sensation of pleasure gives rise to the suffering of change; and the sensation that is neither painful nor pleasant... [text continues]
[They] do not delight in the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*).

[Commentary on the Sub-commentary]: The phrase "In various sūtras and śāstras... briefly indicates the names and numbers. [Commentary on the Sub-commentary]: The phrase "In various... refers to the brief exposition. [Sub-commentary]:

According to the *Satya-śāstra*, everything in this Sahā world is suffering; there is not a single thing that can be enjoyed. Even a burning house or a prison is not comparable [to the suffering of saṃsāra].
As an analogy.

[Commentary on the Sub-commentary] Regarding the Pure Land of Amitābha: in the first section of the initial exposition on the joys of the Pure Land, the first phrase provides a general indication of the objective realm.

[Commentary on the Sub-commentary] Regarding the phrase "the realm is exceptionally sublime": the following five phrases enumerate five characteristics, the first being the excellence of adornment. [Commentary on the Sub-commentary] Regarding the term "sage" (ārya):
[The assembly] consists of worthy ones. [Commentary] Second, the excellence of the principal and the retinue. [Sub-commentary] Hearing the Dharma and awakening to the Way.

[Commentary] Third, the excellence of the Dharma and the Way. [Sub-commentary] A lifespan lasting for kalpas. [Commentary] Fourth, the excellence of the lifespan. [Sub-commentary] Non-retrogression from Bodhi. [Commentary] Fifth, the excellence of realizing the fruit.

[Commentary] Furthermore, there are other pleasures that cannot surpass this; the mere absence of all suffering is already sufficient to be considered pleasant, let alone possessing all such superior matters—how could its bliss ever be exhausted?

Therefore, it is called "ultimate. [Record] The subsequent phrases conclude by clarifying that this is precisely because the wondrous forms and sounds of both the environment and the inhabitants (*āśraya-adhiṣṭhāna*) in that land are all the result of the effortless power of Dharmākara.
The adornment of virtue accords with the nature and conforms to the principle; fundamentally, it has no limit. What is now called "limit" refers to the "limitless.
In contrast, this land is submerged within various manifold sufferings—the three sufferings, four sufferings, five sufferings, eight sufferings—and so forth, which have no boundary;
for this reason, it is also called "the limit."

[Commentary] The *Mūla-sūtra* states: "If, when I attain Buddhahood, the happiness experienced by the devas and humans in my land should not surpass that of a bhikṣu whose outflows are exhausted (*āsravakṣaya*), may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
[Record] Regarding the initial citation from the original vow to provide a direct demonstration, this is followed by a citation from the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning) to encourage practice.
A "bhikṣu whose outflows are exhausted" refers to an Arhat of the four fruits; it means that all their outflows have already been extinguished.
Furthermore, it is a defilement.
[Commentary] Shandao said: "To aspire to be born in that land, one must exert the mind and subdue the self, making the end of life the ultimate goal.
In the present body, this may seem like a minor hardship; yet, as the preceding thought ends and the succeeding thought arises, the long duration of kalpas is eternal."
To enjoy the bliss of unconditioned dharmas until the attainment of Buddhahood, never again passing through birth and death—how joyful this is!
[Commentary] In the subsequent detailed exposition, regarding the land of the dependent retribution, that which is encountered by the ears and eyes does not transcend sound and form.
[Record] In the initial section of the general demonstration within the subsequent detailed exposition, the first four lines provide a general indication of sound and form.
[Commentary] According to the conclusion at the end of the sutra, there are exactly three places that constitute the "adornment of tranquility," which are divided into three sections:
first, the jeweled nets, trees, and ponds consist solely of the adornment of exquisite forms; second, the golden ground, flowers, and music include both the adornments of form and sound;
third, the warbling birds and wind-swept trees consist solely of the adornment of the Dharma-sound. [Record] This refers to the division of the text according to the sutra below.

[Commentary] Therefore, the current topical outline differs entirely from that of the past; one should examine the scriptural text and not merely adhere to old interpretations. [Record] The section beginning with "Therefore" clarifies how the present differs from the ancient.
Mount Gu said: "The manifestation of the signs consists of five parts: 1) railings, nets, and rows of trees; 2) ponds, waters, and pavilions;
3) golden ground and celestial flowers; 4) wondrous and variegated birds; 5) wind-trees and the sound of the Dharma. By means of these...
Because these five kinds constitute adornments, they are called "Pure Awakening that Experiences Only Joy. Regarding the characteristics of these adornments, there are two:
first, the adornment of physical objects and environments; second, the proclamation of the Dharma-sound. As for the first, it has three parts:
(1) railings, nets, and so forth; (2) ponds, pavilions, and so forth; (3) celestial music, golden ponds, and so forth. All of these have been derived from not failing to examine the scriptures.

That this concluding passage contains such omissions and errors truly demonstrates that the present commentary transcends all works past and present; yet, hearing the meaning and being unable to apply it, Confucius lamented this.

[Commentary] Regarding the first section on "Adornment," it is divided into two parts: the first part, ending with "fragrant and pure," enumerates the characteristics of the *śarīra*; the second part concludes [the discussion].
The exposition of the characteristics has two parts. First, from the beginning up to "the Land of Ultimate Bliss," the railings, nets, and rows of trees are cited to reveal the name.
Second, from "Furthermore, Śāriputra" onwards, the ponds, pavilions, and precious lotuses are cited to illustrate the characteristics. Regarding the first part:

Śāriputra, the land of Ultimate Bliss is surrounded on all sides by sevenfold railings, sevenfold nets, and sevenfold rows of trees, all composed of the four precious substances; for this reason, that land is named "Ultimate Bliss."

[Commentary] The first seven phrases demonstrate the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), while the final two phrases conclude by establishing the name. [Sub-commentary] In the sequential explanation of the listed characteristics, regarding "railing" (*vedikā*):

that which runs lengthwise is called a "railing" (*lan*), and that which runs crosswise is called a "crossbar" (*shun*). The *Qieyun* dictionary states: "A fishing-railing at the edge of a flight of stairs."
[Commentary] It is said that the rows of trees are sevenfold in circumference; each tree is eight thousand yojanas high.

Because the rows are aligned with one another without any discrepancy, the branches and leaves of these trees form seven tiers from top to bottom, all draped with nets of pearls, resembling a Buddhist stūpa.
[Record] This initial section explains the rows of trees according to their underlying meaning.
[Commentary] The *Amitābha Sūtra* states: "Exquisite nets of pearls completely cover the trees;
upon each tree there are seven layers of nets, and within each net there are five hundred billion palaces of exquisite flowers. [Record] This next citation from the sūtra serves as proof.
[Commentary] Since there is one row of trees and one row of railings, they are likewise sevenfold. [Record] The phrase "one row" below clarifies the number of layers for the trees and railings.
[Commentary] The net consists of pearl necklaces and is further suspended above the trees. [Record] The phrase "net" below indicates that the pearl net is what is supported by [the trees].

[Commentary]: Thus it is known that these [preceding lines] all serve as a prelude, while the following two lines merely reveal the substance of the tree-railing. [Record]: The phrase "Thus" and below points to the substance of the tree-railing.
[Commentary]: First, gold; second, silver; third, lapis lazuli; fourth, crystal—these constitute the four treasures. [Record]: Next, the four [treasures] are revealed.
The jeweled platform is situated within the four types of jewels that constitute the tree’s railing. △ First, the formal demonstration.
[Commentary] If one follows the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*, the seven-jeweled flowers and petals are fully present;
furthermore, according to the *Larger Sūtra*, the roots, stems, branches, and leaves are interspersed with the seven jewels. [Record] Regarding "If one follows" and below, the staff differs.
[Commentary] Herein, the details are briefly cited; they are found extensively in other texts. [Record] The following clarifies what was omitted.

[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "surrounded on all sides," some say that this is the case for all dwellings of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, and does not mean that there are only seven layers in a single land.
[Record] As for the mention of "surrounded on all sides," the text is seen in both the *Mahāvaipulya* (Great Text) and the new translation.

[Translation of the Scripture]. [Commentary on the Sub-commentary]: The conclusion of the title is easily understood; the subsequent instances of adornment follow this pattern of conclusion. [Commentary on the Record]:

Regarding the phrase "the instances in the conclusion of the title follow this pattern," it means that at the end of the texts concerning the two subsequent locations of adornment, one must likewise conclude by stating: "Therefore, in that land..."
It is named "Ultimate Bliss" (Sukhāvatī), but as the text is abbreviated here, this point is merely indicated. [Commentary:
Regarding the second section on the ponds and pavilions, it is divided into four parts: first, the pond water; second, the stairways along the banks; third, the towers and pavilions atop the stairs;
and fourth, the lotus flowers within the ponds. △ First, concerning the pond water:
Furthermore, Śāriputra, in the Land of Ultimate Bliss there are ponds made of the seven treasures, filled with water possessing the eight meritorious qualities;
the bottoms of these ponds are entirely covered with ground of golden sand.

[Commentary] Regarding the "ponds of the seven treasures": there are eight such ponds there, all composed of the seven treasures. [Record] The explanation of the pond pavilions follows that of the ponds.
Within the water, the number of ponds is first indicated. [Commentary:
The water within these ponds is also the color of the seven treasures and is called the "eight meritorious qualities": first, clarity; second, coolness;
third, sweetness; fourth, lightness and softness; fifth, moisture; sixth, tranquility; seventh, the removal of hunger and thirst; and eighth, the promotion of growth.
The various sense-faculties. [Commentary] Next, the substance of the ponds is shown.

[Sub-commentary] Within the heart of each pond, there is a King of Wish-fulfilling Jewels from which water issues forth and flows into the pond. [Commentary] The phrase "Within each" indicates the source of the water.
[Commentary] Regarding "the ground strewn with golden sand," the *Amitābha-sūtra* (Guan jing) states: "The beds beneath the channels are all made of various colored diamond sands.
[Record] The passage following "gold" indicates that the bottom of the pond is also seen in the *Guan jing*.
[Commentary]: Among the two [features], the stairways on the four sides are composed of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal.
[Commentary]: The steps and pavements are likewise made of these four jewels.
[Commentary: The pavilions of the three-fold clarity are arrayed with the seven treasures.
Above them are pavilions likewise adorned with gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, musaragalva, red pearl, and agate.
[Commentary] The *Amitābha Sūtra* states that in each realm of the land of various jewels, there are five hundred billion jeweled towers.

[Sub-commentary] Since the scriptural text regarding these towers and pavilions merely mentions that "there are towers above," this citation from the *Amitābha Sūtra* is used to demonstrate their specific number.
[Commentary]: *Vaidūrya* is the Sanskrit term; here it is translated as "not far away.
Because this jewel is produced on a mountain not far from the city of Vārāṇasī, it is so named. [Record]: *Vaidūrya* is fully called *vaiḍūrya*.
[Commentary]: *Sphaṭika* is also called *sphāṭika*; this is translated as "water-jade" or "crystal. [Record]: *Sphaṭika* is properly called *sphāṭikā*; its appearance is...
It somewhat resembles the crystal of this region, though it differs in having two colors, red and white. [Commentary] "Carpagha" (車磲) and those following are all Chinese terms;
as for "carpa," it refers to the rim of a chariot wheel. [Record] *Carparaka* (車渠), in Sanskrit, is called *musāragalva*, which translates as "blue-white precious stone.
The *Shangshu Dazhuan* states: "The great *baei* (shell) is like the *qu* (rim) of a large chariot."

The "rim" (wǎng) refers to the base outside the wheel. [Commentary] Regarding the *rakta-maṇi* (red pearl), the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states that it is produced by red insects, as the substance of the pearl itself is red.
[Record] The Sanskrit for *rakta-maṇi* is *padmarāga*, which means "red-light pearl.

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that pearls are found within the bellies of fish, inside bamboo, and within the heads of snakes; they do not originate solely from the embryos of oysters. [Commentary] *Aśmagarbha* (agate)...
The Dharma Master Nan Ying said: "The color of this jewel is red, like agate. [Commentary] Agate is called *musāragalva* in Sanskrit;
the new translations call it *aśmagarbha*, which means "matrix-jewel" (*zàngchǔ*) or is translated as "womb-treasure" (*tāizàng*).
This jewel is named after its firmness and solidity.

[Commentary] The *Mūla-sūtra* states: "If, when I attain Buddhahood, from the ground up to the celestial palaces and towers in the void, the ponds, streams, flowers, and trees were all composed of countless various jewels and hundreds of thousands of kinds of incense, such that their adornments would be marvelous and surpass those of all devas and humans.
[Sub-commentary] This present sutra mentions only the seven jewels; furthermore, it cites the *Mūla-sūtra* regarding the "countless varieties."
The miraculous manifestations of the jewels are not limited [to a single place].
[Commentary: Fourth, the display of lotus flowers.
Within the pond, the lotus flowers are as large as chariot wheels; they are blue with blue light, yellow with yellow light, and red with red light.
"White in color, with white light, subtle, fragrant, and pure.
[Commentary]: There are five aspects: first, shape and size; second, manifest color; third, radiance and flames; fourth, fragrance; and fifth, purity.
These may be seen by comparing them to the text.
[Commentary] If one follows the *Amitābha-sūtra* (Guanjing), within each pond there are sixty billion lotus flowers made of the seven precious substances;

each lotus flower is perfectly round and measures twelve yojanas in diameter. [Record] Among the demonstrations of the distinctions of the lotus flowers, this first section correctly demonstrates those distinctions.
[Commentary] Since it is stated that the seven treasures do not consist of merely four colors. [Record] There are two points: first, the seven treasures differ from the four colors.
[Commentary] Twelve *yojanas* does not refer merely to the wheels of a chariot. [Record] Second, twelve *yojanas* differs from the wheels of a chariot.
[Commentary] However, as for the size of the chariot, it is difficult to establish a fixed standard. Here, the largest does not exceed several feet;
one may take the wheel of a Universal Monarch (*cakravartin*) as the measure. [Record] Thus, regarding the measurement of the chariot wheel below, the initial determination is based on its meaning.
[Commentary]: The *Daśabhūmivibhāṣā* states: "The golden wheel of a Cakravartin King has a thousand spokes, adorned with various rare jewels on its rim, with a hub made of lapis lazuli;
it is fifteen *li* in circumference. Based on this, [the wheel described here] does not even reach half a *yojana*, and this refers only to the smaller variety.

[Record]: The passage below cites the text to demonstrate that the "hub" (*nābhi*) is the horizontal wooden beam inside the wheel. (Note: "Shu" refers to the commentary; "ji" refers to the sub-commentary).
"Thirty spokes converging at a single hub" refers to the place where the spokes meet.
[Commentary] As for why the two sutras differ, Cien (Ci'en) says: "The flowers have large and small sizes; that [sutra] refers to the largest, while this one concerns the smallest.
[Record] To investigate the reason for the difference, the first phrase indicates the discrepancy, while the section following "Cien" harmonizes them.

The mutual expression of compassionate grace—referring to the twelve *yojanas* mentioned in the *Contemplation Sūtra*—is based on the larger figure for the sake of briefly distinguishing the differences between the two sūtras;
however, the Pure Land is infinitely vast and does not merely consist of this number.
[Commentary] Now, according to the *Mahā-sūtra*, the lotuses in the pond are either one *yojana* in size, or even up to a hundred thousand *yojanas*.
[Sub-commentary] Furthermore, by citing the "hundred thousand *yojanas" from the *Mahā-sūtra*, it is verified that [the size] is not fixed.
This so-called *Mahā-sūtra* refers to the two-fascicle *Mahā-amitābha-sūtra* translated by Zhi Qian of the Wu kingdom; it corresponds to the present *Laghu-sūtra*.

[Commentary: Thus we know that the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna differ; the various sūtras are merely cited according to what is appropriate for specific circumstances. [Record: The phrase "Thus" below points out the intended meaning of the sūtra. [Commentary:
One need not use this to compare the superiority or inferiority of the sūtras. [Record: The phrase "not... below" implicitly refutes the errors of the ancients, specifically those of Gushan.
Regarding the two sutras, because they distinguish between the large and small lotuses and determine that the scattered good [karma] is inferior while this sutra is superior,
it is based on the *Amitābha-sūtra* (the *Kuan-ching*).
[Commentary] In the second section, the summary and demonstration:
"Śāriputra, the Land of Ultimate Bliss is thus adorned with such meritorious qualities.

[Commentary] "Thus" refers to the various kinds of exquisite characteristics mentioned above. [Sub-commentary] Regarding the initial explanation of "referring to the various kinds" within the summary:
these are the aforementioned railings, rows of trees, ponds, pavilions, precious lotuses, and so forth.
[Commentary: These are all the adornments of merit accomplished through the cultivation and refinement over kalpas from cause to fruition by Amitābha’s bodhi-vows and practices;
therefore, they are called "adornments of merit. [Record: The section beginning with "These are all" next explains the "adornments of merit."
[Commentary] Therefore, the *Amitābha Sūtra* states: "Such wondrous flowers as these are accomplished through the power of the vows of the Bhikṣu Dharmākara;
all other things are likewise so. How could it be only the flowered throne? The conclusion of the Forty-eight Vows says:
"After that Buddha had established these vows amidst the great assembly, he directed his mind single-mindedly toward adorning the wondrous land," and so forth. [Record] The *Amitābha Sūtra* merely...

The *Miaohua shu* (Commentary on the Sublime Flowers) states that its underlying intent is to provide a comprehensive interpretation; furthermore, it cites the *Daben* (Mahāvaipulya) version as corroborating evidence.
Since it speaks of "adorned sublime lands," what could this not encompass? How could it refer merely to flower-seats?
[Commentary: The subsequent concluding remarks for all the preceding texts are explained in the same manner as this. [Record:

Regarding the phrase "the subsequent conclusions are all explained in the same manner as this," it means that all subsequent summaries concerning the adornment of merit are accomplished through the power of Amitābha’s vows; therefore, they are no longer explained individually, but are included here by way of this single point.
[Commentary] Second, the adornments, which have two parts: first, the listing of the characteristics; second, the summary and demonstration. In the first part, there are three sections:
1. heavenly music; 2. golden ground; 3. heavenly flowers. △ First [section].
Furthermore, Śāriputra, in that Buddha-land celestial music is constantly played.

[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "celestial music is constantly played," according to the *Sūtra of Contemplation* (*Guan jing*), there are three ways in which music is produced. In the visualization of the waters (*shui guan*), it says:
"Ten billion flower-pennants and immeasurable musical instruments serve as adornments; eight kinds of pure winds strike these musical instruments."
Furthermore, the Louguan states that within its towers and pavilions there are immeasurable devas performing celestial music,
and that musical instruments suspended in mid-air sound of themselves without being struck.
[Commentary] According to the sutra cited below, which states that the wind blowing through the jeweled nets produces sounds like those of hundreds of thousands of kinds of music,

we know that the celestial music in that land is not of a single kind. [Record] In the second section on the adornment of celestial music, because it is intended to demonstrate that the celestial music is manifold, the *Amitābha-sukhāvatī-vyūha Sūtra* (Guānjīng) is cited to illustrate this characteristic.
"The ground is made of gold.

[Commentary: Regarding "the ground is made of gold," according to the *Amitābha-sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*, the ground of that land consists entirely of lapis lazuli (*vaiḍūrya*), interspersed with golden cords and further demarcated by boundaries of the seven treasures. What is here referred to as "gold" refers specifically to the surface of the ground.
[This refers to] the adornment of the ground. [Commentary: Within the golden land, that country is composed entirely of lapis lazuli;
the mention here of "golden" refers to the adornment of the ground's surface, not the essential substance of the ground itself.

[Commentary] Regarding the "Flowers of the Three Heavens," there are again three [sections]. First, during the six periods, flowers rain down upon that land; second, they offer abundant flowers as an act of worship;

and third, having completed these offerings, they return to their own lands. △ Regarding the first [section]: [Record] In the phrase "flowers rain down" (*yǔ huā*), the character *yǔ* is pronounced with the departing tone (fourth tone).
The *Shūshū* states: "That which descends from above is called 'rain' (*yǔ*)."
[The land] rains *māndārava* flowers during the six periods of day and night.

[Commentary: Since that land is constantly illuminated by its own radiance and lacks both sun and moon, there is no distinction between day and night; however, for the sake of conforming to the capacities of beings in this region, it is said that there are six periods.
[Commentary] According to the *Mahāvaipulya* version, they take the opening of the lotuses and the singing of the birds as dawn, and the closing of the lotuses and the roosting of the birds as night.

[Record] Regarding "the opening of the lotuses and the singing of the birds," Cien (Ci'en) says: "The blossoming flowers in the golden pond represent the perception of dawn for those born by transformation;
the birds nesting in the jade forest represent the perception of the onset of darkness for the Bodhisattvas."
[Commentary]: "Mandāra" is translated here as "pleasing to the mind," referring to its beauty; it is also translated as "white flower," referring to its color.
Regarding the second [point]:
the sentient beings in that land always, at the clear dawn, each take various wonderful flowers in their robes and baskets to make offerings to those in other directions.
"One hundred trillion Buddhas.
[Commentary: The sentient beings in that land are collectively categorized into nine grades. Regarding "yījì" (衣裓), Zhēndì (真諦) states it is a vessel for holding flowers used in foreign lands.
[Record: Among the offerings, the ancient interpretation of "yījì" also refers to the lapel of a robe.
[Commentary] As soon as one is born in that land, one immediately attains the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) and travels daily to other regions in order to hear the Dharma.
[Commentary] The *Amitābha-sūtra* states: "At that very moment, one is able to fly and travel everywhere throughout the ten directions to serve various Buddhas;
furthermore, one travels through the ten directions to make offerings to the Buddhas and hears the profound Dharma before them. [Record] That is.

Regarding the attainment of supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*), the *Mūla-sūtra* states: "If, when I attain Buddhahood, the humans and devas in my land should not possess supernatural power such that, in a single thought-moment, they cannot travel at least across hundreds of thousands of nayutas of lands, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
If one relies on the passage concerning the lowest grade of rebirth, where one remains within a lotus flower for twelve great kalpas, how could one possibly fly [to other lands] immediately?

The *Xingye shu* (Commentary on the Practice of Merit) states: "This term generally refers to the nine grades; it is spoken of in terms of the general course because serving the Buddha increases merit and hearing the Dharma increases wisdom, thereby accomplishing the two adornments.
[Commentary]: "One hundred trillion" is cited merely as a large number.
[Commentary] Among the three [periods], at the time of eating, he returns to his native land to eat, drink, and practice walking meditation.
[Commentary] "Time of eating" refers to the period before midday. [Record] Regarding the "time of eating," it is the initial fixed period of the day for all Buddhas of the three periods of time.
All [meals] are taken before noon and do not exceed midday.
[Commentary: The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that the palaces, clothing, food, and drink in that land are like the spontaneously appearing objects of the Sixth Heaven (*Ṣaṣṭha-deva*).
When one wishes to eat, bowls and vessels made of the seven precious substances appear naturally before them, and food and drink of a hundred flavors appear spontaneously.
Although these foods appear full and abundant, there is in fact no one who eats them; merely by seeing their colors and smelling their fragrance, they consider it food and are naturally satisfied.

Once the task is finished, the food vanishes, and when the time comes again, it reappears, and so forth. [Commentary] The section below on "Nature" clarifies the sixth heaven, the Paranirmita-vaśavartin (Heaven of Mastery over Others' Emanations).
All enjoyments therein do not require effort or creation; they manifest from the emanations of others.
Therefore, it is named as such.

[Commentary] The *Nanhai Jigui Neifa Zhuan* (Record of Buddhist Practices Sent Home from the Southern Seas) states: "Among the five classes of heavenly beings, both monastics and laity frequently practice *caṅkrama* (walking meditation).
They come and go directly, following only a single path, just like the warp-threads of a loom; hence it is called *caṅkrama*."

[Commentary] The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states that walking meditation (*caṅkrama*) has five benefits: first, one is capable of traveling long distances; second, one is able to engage in contemplation;

third, one suffers little illness; fourth, food is digested; and fifth, one attains the long-term abiding of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). [Sub-commentary] Regarding these benefits of walking meditation: first, a traditional account is cited to show its physical characteristics;

next, the *vinaya* is cited to clarify its benefits. The *Fangzhi* (Record of the Temple) states: "The stone foundation upon which the Buddha practiced walking meditation was fifty paces long and seven [units] high."

The area trodden by [the Buddha’s] feet was all marked with lotus patterns; furthermore, Yijing stated that because both monastics and laypeople frequently practiced *caṅkrama* (walking meditation) throughout the lands of the Five Indias,
there are foundations for the Buddha’s walking meditation at Vulture Peak, beneath the Bodhi tree, within the Deer Park, inside the royal city, and at other sacred sites,
measuring approximately two cubits in width and fourteen or fifteen cubits in length, and rising about two [cubits] in height.
A brick structure about one cubit high was built, topped with stone fashioned into the shape of an opening lotus flower, two inches high and one foot wide;
there were fourteen or fifteen such structures, representing the holy footprints of the Buddha, similar to the walking path (caṅkrama) found at Jetavana Monastery.
"Śāriputra, the Land of Ultimate Bliss is thus adorned with the accomplishment of such meritorious virtues.
[Commentary] The concluding demonstration is the same as before. [Record] Within this concluding demonstration, there are two points identical to the previous section:

first, because it was accomplished through the cultivation and refinement of Amitābha’s vows and practices over kalpas, it is called "adornment of meritorious virtues," and so forth, including the citation of the sūtra.

The explanation is the same as before for both [sections], which must both conclude by stating: "For this reason, that land is named Sukhāvatī. [Commentary: The third section on Adornments also has two parts:
first, listing the characteristics; second, concluding and indicating the meaning. Within the first part, listing the characteristics, there are again two types:
first, up to "the various birds proclaim the holy Dharma"; second, from "the śarīra" onwards, concerning the wind-trees.
Producing wondrous sounds; this section has two parts: first, the formal presentation, and second, the resolution of doubts. △ The formal presentation has three parts:
first, listing the various birds.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, in that land there are always various wonderful and multicolored birds, such as white cranes, *kong* (pheasants),...
The sparrow, the parrot, the śārika, the kalaviṅka, and the *saṃjīva* bird.

[Commentary: These six types are mentioned briefly; the first three are easily identified.
