[Commentary] The answer states: "The Buddha-body is not a [conditioned] mark; its fruit-virtue is so profound and sublime that it does not establish a conventional name, and thus its wondrous essence cannot be manifested.

[Record] In the initial four lines of the answer, the reason for establishing the name is shown generally. "Non-mark" refers to the Dharma-body; as the Sūtra says: "The Buddha’s true Dharma-body is like empty space.
"Fruit-virtue" refers to the Sambhogakāya (Enjoyment Body), which is the internal correspondence above; "responding above and responding below" refers to the Nirmāṇakāya (Response Body).
The Three Bodies and Three Virtues are so lofty as to be unattainable by looking up at them, and so profound as to be unfathomable; they are beyond the reach of the mental power of ordinary beings.
Therefore, auspicious names are established to invoke their essence. Thus, when one invokes even a single name, the Three Virtues are fully manifested.
How could it be said that merely hearing [the Buddha's name] constantly gives rise to negligence or contempt?

[Commentary] Throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time, there are various names [for Buddhas]. [Sub-commentary] The two phrases following "Ten" generally cite the fact that the names of all Buddhas are identical.

[Commentary] How much more so for my Amitābha, who receives sentient beings by means of his name. [Sub-commentary] The two phrases following "How much more so" specifically manifest that Amitābha is supreme.
Superior.
[Commentary] Therefore, by hearing with the ears and reciting with the mouth the boundless holy virtues, one gathers them into the consciousness-mind to serve forever as the seed of Buddhahood;
one immediately eliminates the heavy sins of billions of kalpas and attains the realization of unsurpassed Bodhi. [Record] The following section demonstrates the practice of recitation and upholding.
To increase and expand it constitutes the cause for eliminating sins in the present life; to realize Bodhi constitutes the fruit attained in the future.

[Commentary] "Faithfully knowing" means to understand that this is not a minor root of goodness, but rather a great merit. [Record] "Faithfully" and below trace back the underlying intent to conclude by referring to the preceding section.

[Commentary] The *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* states: "It would be better to undergo the sufferings of hell than to receive the names of the Buddhas; it would not be better to enjoy immeasurable bliss while failing to hear the names of the Buddhas.
[Commentary] The *Bhaiṣajyaguru-vaiḍūryaprabhāsa-sūtra* states: "If the name of that Buddha enters one's ears, there shall be no falling into the evil realms."

In this regard, Ānanda, the realm of the Buddhas is truly difficult to believe; it is entirely through the majestic power of the Tathāgatas that it can be believed and accepted, and not by Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas, except for Bodhisattvas who are in their final birth.
[Commentary] The *Sūtra on the Divination of the Auspicious and the Inauspicious* states:

"Those who wish to be born in a pure land in another direction during the present age should single-mindedly recite the name of the Buddha of that world with focused attention and without distraction.

They will certainly attain birth in that Buddha’s pure land, their roots of goodness will increase, and they will swiftly attain the stage of non-retrogression. One should know that among all roots of goodness, this practice is the most supreme."
[Commentary] The passage beginning with "etc. cites three successive sutras to establish the proof.

[Sub-commentary] The phrase "the names of other Buddhas" means that if even those who merely hear and uphold the names of other Buddhas attain such results, how much more so for me, Amitābha, who possesses original vows? [Commentary] The passage beginning with "other" uses those cases to illustrate this one.

[Commentary] Because people of the degenerate age have heavy obstructions and often neglect the practice of holding the Name, [the author] has cited the sacred words in detail so that there may be no delay or hesitation in one's contemplation.
[Record] The section beginning with "The degenerate age" criticizes the world and clarifies the underlying intent.
[Commentary] Regarding the second [point], "Invoking the Sages":
at the time of that person’s death, Amitābha Buddha, together with the assembly of sages, will appear before them.
[Commentary] The phrase "that person" and below refers back to the aforementioned individual who upholds the Name. [Record] This is the first [section] within "Invoking the Sages."
The first section marks the scriptural text.
[Commentary] Regarding the *Sūtra on the Original Vow of Amitābha* concerning the guidance of those at the end of life, it says:
"If sentient beings of the ten directions sincerely make a vow desiring to be born in my land, at the time of their death, even if I do not appear surrounded by a great assembly..."
"I shall not attain perfect enlightenment before [all beings] stand before me. [Commentary] The reference to "facing those below" can be understood by citing the original vow.
[Sub-commentary] Among the various manifestations of the assembly of holy ones, there are many distinctions. [Commentary] The first two phrases of the following section provide a general heading.

[Commentary]: "Or the True Buddha, the Transformation Buddha, Avalokiteśvara, and Mahāsthāmaprāpta" refers to how they appear according to one's spiritual rank, as detailed in the *Amitāyurdhyāna Sūtra*. [Record]:
The section beginning with "Or the True" specifically demonstrates that the visions perceived differ according to the practitioner's meritorious conduct.

[Commentary] Some claim that seeing the Buddha at the moment of death is an apparition of Māra; others say it is merely the manifestation of one's own karmic reality and that no other Buddha has actually come.

[Commentary] This is because they do not understand that the living being and the Buddha are of one essence, and that the path of resonance and response is mutually interpenetrating. [Record] The section beginning with "This" clarifies the correct view for the multitude.

All Buddhas arise from the same source of awakening; within the minds of the Buddhas, sentient beings newly and constantly create karma, while within the minds of sentient beings, the Buddhas moment by moment realize the truth.
The entirety of the Buddha is the sentient being, and the entirety of the sentient being is the Buddha. Therefore, it is said they are of one essence (*ekatva*).

"Sensation" (*kuan*) belongs to the sentient being, while "response" (*ying*) belongs to the Buddha. Since they are already of one essence, when sentient beings experience sensation, it is naturally... [the response of the Buddha].
The Buddha of the mind and all Buddhas respond to one another because their natures—goodness and evil—are interrelated and their resonance is of a single boundary;
thus it is called "the intersection of the Way.
[Commentary] To obstruct oneself and to obstruct others is a fault that is not slight, as clarified elsewhere. [Record] From here below is the conclusion and the critique, as follows:
A separate clarification regarding the *Jinganshū* (Commentary on the Contemplation Sutra). [Commentary]:
Among the three types of right mindfulness, when such a person’s mind is not inverted at the time of death, they will immediately attain rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss of Amitābha Buddha.
[Commentary] When an ordinary person approaches the end of life, the consciousness lacks a presiding master, and the seeds of good and evil karma all manifest without exception.

[Record] Regarding the initial general demonstration of good and evil within right mindfulness, an ancient master said: "The karmic conditions of good and evil accumulated throughout the past and present all come to press their report at the moment of death.
If evil thoughts increase and flourish at the time of death, then all manner of evils will appear and drag one away."

If, when one is about to be born in an evil realm, wholesome thoughts increase at the moment of death, then all virtues will be realized; because these draw one toward birth in a good realm, it is said that "there is nothing that does not manifest.
[Commentary] Or one may give rise to evil thoughts, or give rise to false views, or produce attachment and longing, or become frantic and deranged. [Record] Or...

Below, the specific characteristics of evil are shown: first, because there is not even a single seed of goodness, one gives rise to evil thoughts; second, because there is no correct faith, one gives rise to false views;
third, because affection and attachment are deep and heavy, one gives rise to clinging and longing; fourth, because one is oppressed by suffering and affliction, one gives rise to madness.

[Commentary]: The various evil characteristics are all termed "perversions" (*viparyāsa*). [Record]: The two lines following "evil" summarize the perversions to manifest what is non-perverse. [Commentary]:

Because one previously recited the Buddha’s name, transgressions were extinguished and obstacles removed; pure karma perfumes from within, while the light of compassion gathers from without, liberating one from suffering.

"One attains bliss in a single kṣaṇa. [Commentary] The following provides a formal explanation of the scriptural text: "The mind is not inverted" refers to reciting the Buddha’s teachings and cultivating the causes.

"Sins are extinguished and hindrances removed" refers to the subduing of malevolent influences. "Pure karma internally perfumes" refers to the arising of goodness. The above sections pertain to compassion through one's own power (*svabala*);
the subsequent three phrases concern seeking birth in the Pure Land by relying on the power of another (*parabala*). Although it is called the power of another, it must necessarily...
Only through one's own power can one bring about the meeting of father and son, like the simultaneous pecking and hatching of an egg;
do not rely exclusively on the power of others and thereby lose your own practice—strive, strive!

[Commentary] The exhortation to generate [the aspiration] in the following passage lies in its benefit. [Record] The exhortation to generate [the aspiration] in the following passage refers to the scripture stating, "I see this as the benefit," and so forth.
The question is whether the pure karma one cultivates exists or does not exist, and in what location it resides. If it does not exist, then one’s mental effort is wasted;
please deign to provide a definitive answer. Although it is said that one adorns the Pure Land, it is not yet clear how one adorns it.

I request instruction on their characteristics: when asking whether at the moment of death one’s rebirth occurs through the conscious spirit (*vijñāna*) departing in secret, or through being gathered and sustained by the Buddha, both positions possess faults.
When asking what the form of the person attaining rebirth is—whether it exists or does not exist—both positions possess faults.

Furthermore, when asking whether the aggregates (*skandha*) of this world perish and the aggregates of that world arise, and whether those aggregates arising there are identical to the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), both positions possess faults.
What is the distinction? I shall briefly set forth five questions to stimulate those of like practice so that they may be free from doubt; their rebirth [in the Pure Land] will then be certain.
[Commentary: Third, the conclusion clarifying the central point:
"Śāriputra, because I see this benefit, I speak these words: if there are sentient beings who hear this teaching, they should..."
"One should make a vow to be born in that land.

[Commentary] "I see this benefit" refers back to the preceding section; thus, these words are spoken to further demonstrate the primary retribution (*vipāka*) described in the previous passage, as can be seen by comparing the text.
[Record] "To conclude and clarify" refers back to the preceding section, which specifically indicates the method of practice.
The passage concerning "single-mindedly reciting the name at the time of death to experience the descent of the Sage and attain rebirth through right mindfulness" reiterates the preceding section;
this refers to the names of the Transformation Master, his retinue, and their majestic adornments, which constitute the "primary retribution.
As the previous conclusion urged, "Sentient beings who hear this should make a vow," here it further states that "those who hear this teaching should..."
Because it concerns the making of vows, it is called "revealing again.

[Commentary] In the third major section, "Exhortation to Believe," there are three sub-sections: first, from the beginning up to "as the Buddha has taught," which exhorts by citing the common praise of all Buddhas;
second, from "If there be someone... onwards, which exhorts by means of the causes and effects of the three periods of time; and third, from "As I am now... onwards, which provides an illustration.

The mutual praise and exhortation of the Buddhas has two parts: first, the benefit of arriving [at this stage], which refers back to the preceding self-praise; second, the subsequent citation of the praises by all Buddhas.
Regarding the first part: [The text continues with the specific content of the praise.]
Śāriputra, just as I now praise the inconceivable merit and benefits of Amitābha Buddha. [Commentary:

As previously stated, the reliance on and the excellence of the primary and secondary [environments] lead to liberation from suffering through the holding of the name. [Record: Third, the exhortation to believe for oneself.

In the praise, the excellence of the primary and secondary [rewards] refers to the adornment of the two types of retribution; that one is liberated from suffering by holding the name is the correct demonstration of the practice method.
[Commentary: It is not that the great compassionate vows and practices of Amitābha—from cause to fruit—do not possess merit and benefit.
"Reaching as far as what the mind thinks and the mouth discusses. [Commentary] This is not yet the formal explanation of the passage on "inconceivable merit" which follows;
it belongs to the current section.

[Sub-commentary] Within the second part, there are two further divisions: first, the exhaustive enumeration of the six directions, and second, the explanation of the sutra text beginning with "What do you think? down to the end.
[Commentary on the Title] Regarding the initial section, only the six directions are listed; however, according to the Tang translation, the ten directions are listed.
[Recorded Notes] In the general demonstration of the Buddha’s praise, the first three phrases correspond to the extensive and abbreviated versions of the two sutras.

[Commentary] Here, it is said that the mention of only the six directions and the four intermediate points is merely a concise way of including [all directions]. [Record] The section beginning with "Now" below demonstrates how the current concise version subsumes the extensive one.

[Commentary] The subsequent names and characteristics of the Buddhas are not explained here. [Record] The final "below" clarifies the explanation of the names of the Buddhas mentioned in the two preceding lines.
The ancient [commentaries] do not provide an explanation.

[Sūtra Commentary: Now, the meaning is detailed through various perspectives: sometimes by way of physical characteristics (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa*), sometimes by taking up words and sounds, sometimes by reference to conduct and practice (*karma*), and sometimes by means of metaphors.
[Sub-commentary: The section beginning with "Now" clarifies the detailed meaning of the present [text].

[Commentary]: In broad outline, there is nothing that is not fully encompassed within the three bodies of the fruit-virtue; though the text may mention them individually, the meaning necessarily includes them all.
[Record]: The phrase "In broad outline" refers to the comprehensive inclusion based on the bodies.

[Commentary] The first section, the Eastern Quarter, is divided into two parts: first, the description of the manifestation of supernatural powers; second, the citation of words of praise. The remaining five quarters follow this same pattern and will not be subdivided further.
Regarding the first part: in the East, there are also the Buddhas Akṣobhya, Merudhvaja, Mahāmeru, and Meruprabhāsa.
The Buddha of Wondrous Sound and other Buddhas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, each from their respective lands,
extended their broad and long tongues, completely covering the trichiliocosm, and spoke words of truth.
[Commentary]: *Akṣobhya* is translated here as "Immovable Dharma-body," because its essence is quiescent and free from transition or change. [Record]:
Among the names of the Buddhas of the eastern direction, this first Buddha is initially explained in terms of his fruition (*phala*).

[Commentary] If one examines them from the perspective of their causes, disparagement and praise, respect and contempt, are identical because they are the same as Suchness (*tathatā*). [Record] Next, this explains the verbal karma of disparagement and praise;
respect and contempt refer to bodily karma. Because the eight winds cannot move them, both self and phenomena are forgotten; hence it is called "identical to Suchness."
[Commentary: Next, three names are listed, all derived from metaphors. Among all mountains, Sumeru is the most supreme; likewise, the *dharmakāya* of the Buddhas transcends all phenomena.
First, regarding "form" (*lakṣaṇa*), its appearance is identical [to the mountain]. Second, regarding "great" (*mahat*), it surpasses the metaphor.
Third, regarding "light" (*prabhā*), light represents wisdom; this encompasses both the *dharmakāya* and the *saṃbhogakāya*. [The Buddha] preaches the Dharma with wondrous sounds.

"Responding according to capacity" refers to the *nirmāṇakāya* (Transformation Buddha). [Commentary] The next three [buddhas] are not necessarily the *dharmakāya* (Dharma-body); they are distinguished from the subsequent Buddha by way of metaphor. It can be seen that the latter Buddha is the *nirmāṇakāya*.

[Sub-commentary] Since the names of five types of buddha-lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges have been briefly listed, it says "such as these. [Commentary] The lands are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
The Buddha is likewise so; because it is impossible to enumerate them all, the term "etc. is used. In the Sanskrit language, this river is called Gaṅgā, also known as Jieṅjiā (Ganges).
Master Yingfan said: "This river flows from the eastern 'Elephant Mouth' of Lake Anavatapta and enters the Eastern Ocean.
Its sand is extremely fine, flowing along with the water; if one scoops it up with the hand," [it remains with the water].

Then, as the sand follows the water away, consider this trichiliocosm: taking a single transformation of the Sahā world as a unit—consisting of one Mount Sumeru, one sun and moon, and one set of four continents, together with the six heavens of the desire realm above and the Brahma worlds above them—this constitutes one world-system.

One thousand such systems is called a "small thousand" (cūḷāsāhasra-lokadhātu); one thousand times a small thousand is called a "middle thousand" (dvisāhasra-madhyama-lokadhātu); and one thousand times a middle thousand...
It is called a "great trichiliocosm," which refers to the three worlds consisting of the four cardinal directions, the four intermediate directions,

the zenith, and the nadir. [Commentary] "Each in their own land" means that at the very time Śākyamuni was preaching this sutra, the Buddhas of the ten directions simultaneously exhorted and praised him,
urging others to believe in this sutra.

[Commentary]: If one considers that the words of all Buddhas are without falsehood, yet because sentient beings have heavy obstructions it is difficult for them to believe, the Buddhas manifest the mark of the tongue to demonstrate the truth of their speech.
[Commentary]: Although the tongues of all Buddhas normally reach up to the hairline, when manifested here, its length and breadth are displayed according to what is appropriate.

"How could the magnitude [of the world] stop at the Great Thousandfold World System? [Commentary] The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* asks: "The World-Honored One possesses great virtue and majestic dignity;
for what reason does he extend his broad and long tongue as if it were a minor physical trait? The answer is:

"Now, wishing to preach the Dharma that is difficult to believe and difficult to understand, he extends the mark of the tongue as proof that [what he says] is necessarily true. It is asked: "Does each [Buddha] extend his tongue within his own land?"

[Question: To whom does this covered great trichiliocosm belong as its sphere of transformation? [Answer: When that Buddha praises it, one thereby knows that this is the sphere of transformation of this Buddha.
[Commentary: Next, he cites the words of praise:
"You sentient beings should believe this praise of the inconceivable merit, which is [the sphere] of all Buddhas..."

*Hunian jing* (The Scripture on Protection and Mindfulness). [Commentary] One should believe that this phrase marks a break. [Sub-commentary] This is the first division of the introductory verses of praise.

[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "Praise below," this refers to the first line of the scripture’s title itself; the preceding part points to what was spoken by Śākyamuni, while the following two lines refer to [the subsequent content].
As explained in the subsequent scriptural text [the *Commentary*]: "The title below indicates the main heading, consisting of three phrases in total.

The first phrase of eight characters, 'Expounded by Śākyamuni,' refers to the preceding scriptural text concerning the adornments of the Dharma-body and the physical realm, as well as the practice of reciting the name and cultivating the Dharma.
The following two phrases, 'The Name extols inconceivable merit,' refer to what follows, namely, the Buddhas of the six directions."
An inquiry is raised as to why this is titled "Protected and Mindfully Kept by All Buddhas," and so forth;
yet, while this title was spoken by the Buddhas of the six directions, its opening phrase—"Just as I now praise the inconceivable merit of Amitābha Buddha"—is the very speech of Śākyamuni himself.
The Sūtra states: "As I now praise the inconceivable merit of Amitābha Buddha."
[Commentary: The remaining five sections following the title are all explained in the same manner as this. [Record: "The remaining" below refers to the preceding explanation of the title;
since the subsequent sections follow the same pattern, they are not explained again.
[Commentary]: Second, regarding the southern direction:

Śāriputra, in the worlds of the southern direction, there are Buddhas such as Candrasūryapradīpa, Yaśasprabha, Mahārciskandha, Merupradīpa, and Anantavīrya—Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, each of whom [resides] in their respective [worlds].
That land produces the mark of the broad and long tongue, which completely covers the trichiliocosm as he speaks words of truth.

[Commentary] The three—sun, moon, and lamp—all dispel darkness; alternatively, they correspond respectively to the three bodies (trikāya), or they serve as single metaphors for the virtue of wisdom (jñāna-guṇa).

[Record] Among the first five Buddhas of the south, the first is based on metaphor and has two meanings. First, it corresponds to the three bodies: the sun is the Dharma-body (dharmakāya); the moon is the... [text breaks off].
The Sambhogakāya is itself the Dharmakāya, or it may be correlated with the three wisdoms; since the one is the three, it serves as a single metaphor for the virtue of wisdom.
[Commentary] "Light of Renown" means that one's fame pervades the ten directions, like light shining everywhere. [Record] The second section treats both the Dharma and the metaphor together.
[Quotation].

[Commentary]: Regarding "Great Blazing Shoulders" (*Mahārciskandha*), in terms of physical marks, it refers to the radiant flames upon both shoulders; in terms of wisdom, it refers to the dual illumination of the ultimate and conventional truths.
[Record]: The third point, the radiant flames on the two shoulders, manifests the two wisdoms of the ultimate and the conventional.
[Commentary] "Sumeru Lamp" refers to the mountain-lamp, which is a metaphor for the two bodies: the Dharma-body and the Reward-body. [Record] The fourth, "Mountain Lamp," uses both metaphors:
the mountain rising high represents the virtues of the Dharma-body, while the lamp’s ability to dispel darkness represents wisdom.
[Commentary: "Immeasurable Diligence" is named after its activity; it is the skillful means for delivering sentient beings, never for a moment flagging.

The immeasurability of compassion and wisdom regarding sentient beings is likewise so. [Record: The fifth, Immeasurable Diligence, manifests the function of liberation through practice in response to the capacities of beings.
"You sentient beings, you should believe in this Sutra on the Praise of the Inconceivable Merit and the Protection and Mindfulness of All Buddhas.
[Commentary] Third, within the Western Quarter.
"Śāriputra, in the western world-system there are Buddhas such as Amitāyus,
Amitābha, Amitadhvaja, Mahāprabha, Mahārcis, Ratnākṣa, and Vimalaprabha— Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—
who each, in their respective lands, extend their broad and long tongues to completely cover the trichiliocosm and speak words of truth."
"True words.
[Commentary] The first three are all termed "immeasurables": the first is lifespan; the second is the marks and signs (lakṣaṇa-vyañjana);
and the third is the Dharma-body (dharmakāya) realized, which is supreme and thus likened to a banner. [Record] Regarding the lifespans and marks of the seven Buddhas of the West, one or two...
All [these] follow from the third banner, "Requiting Virtue," because the Dharma-body is most supreme and its manifestation is lofty and eminent.

[Commentary on the *Sūtra*]: "Great light" and "great brilliance" both serve as metaphors for the Buddha’s wisdom in its self-cultivation and its transformation of others, destroying obstacles and eliminating delusions. [Commentary on the *Record*]:
Both "great light" and "great brilliance" use light to manifest the light of wisdom; the light of wisdom can destroy darkness, and the power of wisdom can sever delusions.

[Commentary] "Precious marks" (ratnalakṣaṇa) refers to the physical characteristics and secondary signs (*lakṣaṇānuvyañjana*) of a Response-Buddha (*nirmāṇabuddha*), which are as precious and noble as jewels. [Record] This passage cites both the phenomenon and its metaphor;
his marks are upright and majestic, like a jewel that is honored and noble.

[Commentary] "Pure Light" (Jingguang) is also the Dharmakāya and Sambhogakāya. [Record] "Pure Light" means that the light of wisdom is purely immaculate, such that the darkness of afflictions is eliminated without remainder.
[Commentary] Question: If the initial Amitāyus is identical to Amitābha, then it would not be appropriate for the text to exhort and praise him as "himself. Answer: ...

There are many who share this same name; it must certainly not be the Amitābha formed from the Dharma-treasury of Sukhāvatī. [Commentary] Next, in resolving doubts, one should not engage in self-praise;

therefore, in the response, it is shown that just as Amitābha’s intention was revealed in reply to a question, one must know that all Buddhas possess identical names and titles, such as the two groups of Buddhas named Sūryapradīpa and Candrapradīpa mentioned in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, or the Buddhas named Maṇidhvaja.
There are eight hundred billion Buddhas, all named Śākyamuni and so forth.
You sentient beings should have faith in this *Sūtra on the Inconceivable Merit of Praise and the Protection and Mindfulness of All Buddhas*.
[Commentary]: Fourth, regarding the northern direction:

In the northern world-systems, there are Buddhas such as Arciṣkandha, Varaghoṣa, Durjayottara, Sūryagarbha, and Jālinīprabha—Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—who each, in their respective lands, manifest the broad and long [tongue].
The mark of his tongue completely covers the trichiliocosm as he speaks words of truth.
[Commentary] Jvālāṃsa (Flame-Shoulder) is the same as the previous one, except that the character "Great" (大) is absent; Suvaraghoṣa (Most Victorious Sound) is the same as Susvara (Sublime Sound).
[Record] For the first two Buddhas of the north, the two fingers are the same.

[Commentary] "Difficult to perish" means that the Dharma-body is firm and impenetrable, and thus cannot be destroyed. The character *cu* (殂) is pronounced as *xù* (敘), or alternatively as *jū* (疽), meaning "to destroy.
[Record] Third, "the Dharma-body is indestructible" means that the Dharma-body of Vairocana cannot be thwarted or destroyed by any demons whatsoever.

[Commentary] "Born of the Sun" means that it is like the morning sun of the world, which dispels the darkness and gloom. [Record] Among the four, this refers to the merit of the Response Body (nirmāṇakāya), which is like the sun illuminating the world.
[Commentary] "Luminous Net" means that the dharma-gates reflect one another like the net of Indra. [Record] The fifth is the Luminous Net Samādhi.
This Dharma gate is like a net of Indra’s jewels, with each reflecting the others.
You sentient beings should have faith in this Sutra on the Inconceivable Merit of Praise, which is protected by the mindfulness of all Buddhas.
[Commentary: Regarding the fifth direction below:
in the world-systems of the lower direction, there are Buddhas such as Siṃha Buddha, Yaśas Buddha, Nāma-prabhāsa Buddha, Dharma Buddha, Dharma-dhvaja Buddha, and Dharmadhara Buddha;
these and other Buddhas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, each appear in their respective lands.
The mark of the broad and long tongue completely covers the trichiliocosm as he speaks words of truth.
[Commentary] As for the lion, because he is the most honored among all sages, he is compared to the king of beasts.

Furthermore, just as when a lion roars once and all other beasts perish upon hearing it, so too do the Māras and heterodox teachers vanish when the Buddha preaches the Dharma. [Record] This is the first of the six marks of the Buddha listed below.

From the two meanings of the analogy: first, because the *dharmakāya* is unsurpassed, it is likened to a king; second, because the *nirmāṇakāya* preaches the Dharma to benefit sentient beings, demons and non-Buddhists are subdued.

[Commentary] "Renown" (*kīrti*) and "light" (*prabhā*) have the same meaning as explained previously. [Record] The second and third points are the same as before; now, regarding the one Buddha in the south...
[The title] is divided into two parts. [Commentary:

*Dharma* is translated as "Dharma" (the Teaching). When used alone, it refers to the Dharmakāya realized [by the Buddha], because it serves as the norm and sustainer (*dhṛti*) of the myriad transformations.
Next, it is called "Banner" (*dhvaja*), because it rises high above all other things. Third, it is called "Sustainer" (*dhara*), because it maintains and upholds [reality] eternally. [Record: Four.

Although these six flowers differ from those in the Sanskrit version, they are none other than the Dharma-body; the fifth [phrase] cites both the dharma and its metaphor, which is likewise a virtue of the Dharma-body.
You sentient beings should believe in this praise of inconceivable merit, which is that which all Buddhas have...
The *Ratnaketu-dhāraṇī-sūtra*.
[Commentary]: Regarding the six directions above, in the worlds of the zenith, there are the Buddhas Brahmaghoṣa, Nakṣatrarāja, Gandhottama, and Gandhaprabha.

all these good sons and good daughters are collectively protected and remembered by all Buddhas, and they all attain...

[Commentary: The Chapter on Śrī-Ābhāsvara states: "The Tathāgatas of the ten directions cherish and remember sentient beings, just as a mother remembers her child."

because she protects through the two minds of compassion and mercy, she prevents Māra from disturbing her great compassion;

because she is mindful, she prevents her great kindness from being lost or regressed. There are four kinds of Māras: the Māra of the five aggregates (*skandha-māra*), the Māra of afflictions (*kleśa-māra*), and the Māra of death (*mṛtyu-māra*).

Regarding the phrase "the Māra of the devas" (*devaputramāra*) and the current mention of "harassment" (*yǎo*): this refers specifically to the *devaputramāra*. Although the two metaphors cited from the sūtras and śāstras differ, their meaning is one and the same.
[Commentary: *Anuttara* is translated here as "unsurpassed" (*wúshàng*). *Samyak* means "right" or "correct" (*zhèng*). *Sambodhi* means "perfect enlightenment" (*zhèngbó*).

[Commentary] Ordinary beings on the stage of thinness (*bhūmi*) are bound by karma and afflictions, transmigrating through the five destinies for hundreds of thousands of myriads of kalpas.

[Commentary] Suddenly hearing of the Pure Land and aspiring to seek rebirth therein, one who recites the Name even for a single day shall transcend to that land;

protected by the mindfulness of all Buddhas, one proceeds directly toward Bodhi. [Record] From "Suddenly" (*hu*) onwards, this explains how current practice moves the Buddha to respond, specifically clarifying the meaning of his protective mindfulness.
[Commentary] It may be said that such an opportunity is difficult to encounter in ten thousand kalpas and is met but once in a thousand lifetimes.

[Sub-commentary] Within the exhortation to believe, "belief" (*śraddhā*) is the mind that is capable of believing; "teaching" (*śāsana*) is the dharma that is the object of belief. This encompasses both.

"Born now, one should vow for this life; currently wishing, one shall be born in the future.

[Commentary] This is intended to demonstrate that in the Pure Land, there is no fear of not being born provided one has made a vow; if one has a vow, birth is certain and there is no possibility of error.

[Record] The passage beginning with "intended to" correctly shows the meaning of generating a vow within the sutra to induce rebirth. Regarding "if one has a vow, one will certainly be born," the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* says:

This is because in this [defiled] land, there is the fault of falling back despite one's progress in cultivation; by contrast, the purity [of the Pure Land] is thereby revealed.
"The earth alone shall not retreat.

"Be born in that land.

[Record] In the section on the exhortation to conclude, the *Sūtra* states: "The great ocean of the Buddha-dharma: faith is that by which one enters, and wisdom is that by which one crosses over."

This is the teaching that transforms and guides through both belief and non-belief; for those who, according to their own karmic conditions, willingly submit to suffering like being smeared with mud or cast into fire and charcoal—where "mud, mire, fire, and charcoal" is a metaphor for the three evil realms—the very failure of their lack of faith serves to manifest the benefits of being able to believe.
[Commentary: Regarding the third section, "The Mutual Praise of All Buddhas," there are two parts. First, "I praise all Buddhas"; second, "All Buddhas below praise me.
**First Part:** Śāriputra, just as I now extol the inconceivable merit of all Buddhas...
[Commentary]: "As I do now," and so forth, refers back to the previous section on the exhortation to have faith through the six directions. [Record]:

Within the section where the Buddhas praise one another, this initial phrase "I praise the Buddhas" is identified by the Commentary as referring back to the exhortation to have faith via the six directions.
Furthermore, while the Tathāgatas of the six directions exhorted sentient beings to believe and accept the sūtra spoken by Śākyamuni, these words are all Śākyamuni praising Amitābha.
Now, as for the statement "praising all Buddhas," although each Buddha individually praises Śākyamuni in their own lands,
the sentient beings of this land have no knowledge of it; nevertheless, because it is Śākyamuni who manifests this, it is [Śākyamuni] who, in turn, praises all the Buddhas.
[Commentary: Within the second [section], there are again two parts. First, the presentation of their words of praise; one should know that the following two [parts] demonstrate their sincerity.
Regarding the first:
those Buddhas and others also proclaim my inconceivable merit, speaking these words: "Śākyamuni..."
The Muni Buddha is able to perform a most difficult and rare feat: amidst the five corruptions of this Sahā world—
the corruption of the eon, the corruption of views, the corruption of afflictions, the corruption of sentient beings, and the corruption of life—
he has attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and preaches for all sentient beings this Dharma that is difficult for all the worlds to believe.

[Commentary: "Śākyamuni" translated as "Able Benevolent One" (Nengren) refers to Great Compassion manifesting in response; "Munī" translated as "Silent Sage" (Jimo) refers to Wondrous Wisdom merging with the Ultimate Truth.
When these two are united as the Buddha, the three bodies (tri-kāya) are complete. [Sub-commentary: In praising the title of our Buddha, "Śākya" is his clan name and "Munī" is his personal name.
Both are translations from Sanskrit into Chinese (Huā), which clearly reveal the Dharma-body, Reward-body, and Response-body.
Great compassion descending in response is the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body); wondrous wisdom manifesting as retribution is the world-illuminating *dharmakāya* (truth body).
[Commentary: Because others cannot produce them, they are extremely difficult to bring forth; because the entire world has not yet seen them, they are rare.
[Commentary]: The following two difficulties are: first, practicing and attaining Buddhahood in this degenerate age; second, preaching this Dharma-gate for the sake of all sentient beings.
[Record]: Regarding the general demonstration of what is extremely difficult: the application of all-worldly omniscience is not considered extremely difficult or rare;
rather, it is the attainment of the Way and the realization of sainthood within a degenerate age, and furthermore, being able to provide instruction therein, that is truly so.
The Dharma-gate for sentient beings to be reborn [in the Pure Land] may be considered extremely difficult and rare.

[Commentary: Regarding the first [point], *Sahā* is also called *So-ho*; this is translated as "Endurance" (*Kannin*). [Sub-commentary: *Sahā* is a Sanskrit term with two phonetic variations, *Sa* and *So*, which are both uniformly translated as "Endurance."
[Commentary] The *Karunāpuṇḍarīka Sūtra* states: "Because these sentient beings endure the three poisons and all afflictions.

[Sub-commentary] The two sūtras cited here differ in their treatment of the singular and the plural when explaining the meaning; the former refers to sentient beings who are deeply attached to turbid evil and willingly endure various sufferings.
[Commentary] According to the *Buddhakṣetrasūtra*, there are two meanings. The first meaning is as explained above. The second states:
"Therein are those who practice the Bodhisattva vehicle, who have accomplished patience (*kṣānti*) and protect sentient beings while skillfully disciplining themselves.

Even if others inflict harm upon them, they are able to endure it all and never become lax; therefore, it is called 'Endurance' (*Kṣānti*). [Record] This subsequently refers to the Bodhisattva’s transformation of others.
Even when encountering adversity while practicing patience and wisdom, one’s great compassion never abandons [sentient beings].
[Commentary] The five turbidities are also called the five dregs; they are termed "evil" because they enable the full commission of the ten unwholesome karmas.
[Commentary] Among the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*), "turbidity" means impurity; "sediment" means foulness; and "evil" means unwholesomeness.
Because evil karma is not pure, it is called turbidity and sediment. The *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* says:
"For example, if sand and soil are thrown into clear water, the soil loses its obstructive nature and the water loses its clarity, becoming turbid and murky."
[Commentary: "Kalpa" (劫) is called *kalpa* in Sanskrit; this is translated here as "period of time. The four subsequent turbidities (*kaṣāya*) gather during this period.
From the time when human lifespan decreases to twenty thousand years, one enters the turbidity of the kalpa (*kalpa-kaṣāya*).

[Commentary: "Views" refers to the five sharp afflictions (*pañca-tīkṣṇa-anuśaya*): the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*), extreme views (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*), false views (*mithyā-dṛṣṭi*), attachment to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and attachment to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*).
[Commentary: "Afflictions" refers to the five dull afflictions (*pañca-mṛdu-anuśaya*): greed (*rāga*), hatred (*dveṣa*), delusion (*moha*), pride (*māna*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*).
[Commentary] "Sentient beings" (sattva) refers to the provisional designation of "sentient beings" formed by grasping the aggregates (*skandha*) as a person.
[Commentary] "Life-force" (*jīvitendriya*) refers to that which arises and perishes moment by moment, hastening the years and shortening the lifespan. [Record] *Kalpa* is translated as "time-period.

The *Karunāpuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "When the human lifespan was sixty thousand years, it decreased by one year every hundred years until it reached thirty thousand; at that point, it had not yet become turbid."

When the human lifespan was twenty thousand years, the age of turbidity (kaṣāya) first began; since Śākyamuni appeared in the world when the human lifespan was one hundred years, the nature of this turbidity can be understood.
The kalpa-turbidity is the general category, while the four types of turbidity are the specific ones. The second and third [turbidities] pertain generally to those of sharp and dull faculties.

As for the ten fetters (*anuśaya*), "view of a self" (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) arises from falsely calculating within name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*). "Extreme view" (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) is the attachment to a biased mind.
Because one treads upon the middle way, those with wrong views take up principles with a distorted mind and thus practice as icchantikas;

those with attachment to precepts either hold to the wrong precepts of external paths or, even regarding the Buddha’s precepts, stubbornly cling to them with partiality; those with attachment to views mistakenly perceive nirvana;

that which leads to insatiable grasping is called greed; that which is characterized by anger and a lack of compassion is called hatred; and that which is deluded and lacks clarity is called ignorance.
To rely on oneself and look down upon others is called *māna* (conceit). To have a deluded mind that deviates from principle and is hesitant or indecisive is called *vicikitsā* (doubt).
The first five [afflictions] are termed "sharp" (*li*) because they are light and easily severed; the latter five are termed "dull" (*duan*) because they are heavy, turbid, and difficult to sever.

The fourth [category], namely the four aggregates (*skandha*), is a collection of phenomena provisionally designated as a "sentient being. Among these five, that which "hastens the years and shortens the lifespan" refers to the retribution of momentary arising and ceasing.
Because the limit [of his lifespan] is not long, the *Karunāpuṇḍarīka-sūtra* further states that the Bodhisattva Śāntamati asked the Buddha:
"The worlds of all other Buddhas are pure and subtle; for what causes and conditions does our World-Honored One now attain equal and perfect enlightenment in this world of five turbidities?
The Buddha replied: "It is because of the power of my vow of great compassion that I have taken up this defiled and evil world."
"It is merely an impure land.

[Commentary] In the second objection, the Dharma-gate of mindfulness of the Buddha is addressed. [Record] Within the first part of the second objection regarding the preaching of the Dharma, from the beginning up to "rebirth," the manifestation of the Dharma's subtlety and its gathering of capacities is shown;
the first two phrases repeat the nature of the Dharma.

[Commentary] It does not distinguish between the foolish and the wise; it does not select between the noble and the lowly; it does not consider the duration of time, whether long or short; and it does not choose between the good and the evil. [Record] The four phrases below encompass the capacities of those who are recipients [of the teaching].
"Foolish and wise" refers to the difference in the sharpness or dullness of their innate nature. "Noble and lowly" refers to the difference in the strength or weakness of their karmic retribution.
"Long and short" refers to the difference in the depth or shallowness of their merit. "Good and evil" refers to the difference in the excellence or deficiency of their conduct.

[Commentary] It refers exclusively to those who, despite facing evil signs at the moment of death, achieve rebirth through ten recitations of the Buddha's name based on firm vows and fierce faith. [Sub-commentary] Regarding the three phrases beginning with "Exclusively":

these describe the mode of practice that brings about rebirth. "Evil signs at the moment of death" refers to the passage in the *Contemplation Sūtra* concerning the lowest of the low grade of rebirth, where the fires of hell all arrive at once.
"Rebirth through ten recitations" refers to the fulfillment of ten recitations within that same lowest grade of rebirth.
[Commentary] This is the method for ordinary, ignorant, and fettered beings of the lowest sort—such as butchers and wine-sellers—to transcend [samsara] and attain Buddhahood in a single moment;
it can truly be called something that is extremely difficult for all the world to believe. [Record] This precisely clarifies the meaning of its being difficult to believe.
"Fettered" (jùbó) means that the three delusions are still fully present; "butcher" (tú) refers to slaughtering livestock, while "wine-seller" (gū) refers to selling liquor—such are the evil ones.
That a person can, by merely ten recitations, attain transcendence—is this not difficult to believe?
[Commentary] Second, regarding the revelation of reality:
"Śāriputra, you should know that in this world of five turbidities, I have performed this difficult task and attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi..."
To preach this dharma, which is difficult to believe, for the sake of all the world by means of *samyaksambodhi*, is exceedingly difficult.
[Commentary] By taking up the two preceding difficulties, it is shown that the praise bestowed upon the Buddhas is not in vain, with the intent that sentient beings hear it and accept it with faith.
[Record] In the "Manifesting the Reality" section, both difficulties are stated according to worldly sentiments; subsequently, it is called "exceedingly difficult."

When one compares the difficulty of attaining Buddhahood in this turbid and evil age with the ease of being born in the Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss through even a small amount of merit from reciting the Buddha’s name, the latter is far more remarkable.

[Commentary] Third, the section on propagation: as the formal exposition has concluded, the assembly joyfully accepts and maintains it, transmitting it from person to person until it is spread everywhere.
Because it extends throughout the four seas and for ten thousand generations, it is therefore circulated by means of its dissemination among the multitude.

[Commentary] In the first section of the "Circulation" (liú-tōng), the initial eight lines explicitly reveal the intent of circulation; the following section reiterates and explains the scriptural text.

Within this, the phrase "the assembly joyfully receives and upholds" refers to the assembly listed in the preceding introduction, whose influence pervades the four seas in horizontal breadth. It "extends" (chuí) [throughout].
To establish this profound cause for ten thousand generations, it was disseminated after the assembly had dispersed,
as other sutras may differ. When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, the Venerable Śāriputra, the bhikṣus, and all those in the world— gods, humans, asuras, and others—
hearing what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced, accepted it with faith, prostrated, and departed.

In the layered explanation, the four categories are the devas, nāgas, spirits, and ghosts; the previous introduction spoke of them collectively as "immeasurable multitudes."

Consequently, he made a vow to abstain from alcohol, which is why it is also translated as "Lacking Uprightness," referring to its coarse appearance and sparse form.

This is subsumed under the superior grade of the asura realm within the destiny of devas.

one attains receptive faith because one ought to put it into practice.

This record was composed by Master Zu’ān during the Chunxi era. Upon reaching the section concerning the manifestation of the Buddha in the East, he showed signs of illness and set down his pen;
subsequently, he passed away, unable to complete the full volume. Those who heard of this did not fail to lament and regret it. Although...

The *Yuanxiu* and *Chaoyuan* commentaries have circulated throughout the world, yet practitioners of various regions have found fault with their literary style and principles, as these were not fully clarified;

consequently, few have adopted them, and by extension, this present commentary has also fallen into obscurity. While I was residing at Qingyuan Hermitage on Mount San, during the course of my lectures, two or three disciples requested that I continue the work.
Out of sincerity, I have produced this "reckless" draft, though it may bring blemish upon what came before.

residing in Sānshān Lǐ of Ānqī Guǎn, Tàichōu Xiāng, Dìnghǎi Xiàn, Dinghai Prefecture, Great Song State.

In honor of the Buddha, Lady Wang (courtesy name Cai Zhongyu), née Bai-er-shi-si-niang Miaoyi, along with Jia Chun and others, have donated thirty *guan* from their official stipends to commission artisans to carve this complete set of recorded texts.
By the merit of this deed, may the family members be protected and peace be secured; may all auspiciousness be accomplished; may blessings and longevity increase in this present life;
and at the end of life, may they be reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*). May the four debts of gratitude and all beings in the three realms of existence partake in the Dharma.

Recorded on the day of the full moon in the fourth month of the tenth year of Jiading, the Great Year Dingchou, when those of both enmity and kinship within the realms have together departed from saṃsāra and been reborn in the Pure Land.
